In the old house at the corner of Maple and 3rd, where the paint peeled like shedding snakeskin and the porch sagged from years of sighing under winter snow, lived Mr. Statler, or Old Statler as the children called him with the kind of wary reverence that old men tend to inspire in young hearts unacquainted with the wear of time. He had not always been old, though to those who saw him now, with his knobby hands and his beard gone bristly white, it seemed impossible that he had ever been any other way. He moved slowly, it is true, as if every step cost him a decision, but his eyes, at certain moments, could flash with the green quickness of a spring-lit forest, and then one glimpsed the man he had been, living still beneath the folds of age.

Those who delivered the mail spoke quietly of the inside of the house, saying it smelled of pipe tobacco and oiled leather, and that the walls bore maps—dozens of them—of cities and coastlines, rivers and mountain chains, as if Old Statler was keeping track of the world’s changing face for some purpose known only to himself. The children, when their balls or kites escaped into his yard, would sometimes dart up onto the porch and peer through the wavy glass, and on good days, Old Statler would open the door and invite them in without speaking, his gesture crooked but warm, to retrieve whatever they had lost. Sometimes he would let them linger, and point out a country with a gnarled finger, muttering, “Here be tigers, methinks,” or “In the valleys here, the air smells like honey and thunder.” The children would giggle, unsure if he was teasing or telling the truth, and scamper away when they felt the weight of his gaze.

It was said by some—those who remembered him as the young man who had once left town with a knapsack and a grin as wide as the river—that Old Statler had lived a life that ran richer and deeper than most, and that he kept those maps as a kind of journal, each line and symbol a memory pressed flat and silent for safekeeping. There were rumors that he had fought in wars, that he had sailed on ships with names as forgettable as dreams, that he had loved and lost and loved again, all while the rest of the town went about its cycles of planting and reaping, loving and dying, as ordinary as the seasons themselves.

His daughter sometimes visited, driving up from the city in a car so new and polished it looked absurd parked beside the faded clapboard. She would bring groceries, sometimes a pie or a tin of coffee, and would sit with Old Statler on the porch, trying in her careful and adult way to persuade him to move in with her, “just for a little while, Dad, until it’s easier.” But he would only smile, his face softening like wet clay, and say, “There are still places on the map I’ve yet to visit, even if only with my mind.” She would sigh, not really understanding—how could she?—yet love and resignation mingled in her eyes as she kissed his forehead and returned to her world of schedules and elevators.

The people in town marked the passing of Old Statler’s days as one marks the seasons, by small changes and quiet rhythms. They saw him trimming the wild roses in spring, standing at the edge of the sidewalk in summer, arm raised in greeting as children biked past, raking leaves in autumn’s chill, and, in the winter, sitting at the window with a lamp burning, casting his shadow like a watchman’s silhouette over the snow. Some thought him lonely, but he did not seem so; rather, he seemed to be living in a time with different measures, where a day could hold the memory of a whole other life, and where the silent companionship of a map or a fading photograph was enough.

Once, when I was a boy, I lost a marble in his yard, a swirl of green and gold that I cherished more than seemed reasonable. I stood uncertain at the foot of his steps, the late light slanting across the porch, and Old Statler appeared as if conjured by my longing. Without a word, he led me to the overgrown hydrangeas, bent with surprising grace, and plucked the marble from the tangle. The streets were gray and damp that morning, the kind of day when the clouds press so low over the city you imagine you could reach up and let your hand vanish into them. Pavel let himself drift along the curb, hands stuffed deep into the pockets of his worn coat, his mind moving as heavily as his feet. He hadn't slept, not really, and every time he closed his eyes in the night, he saw the same narrow room, the same pale face behind the window. 

He supposed he was a fool. Razumihin told him so often enough—always with a kind of affectionate exasperation, as if that would soften it. "You overthink everything, Pasha," he'd say, clapping a friendly hand against Pavel’s back. "You should let things happen." Pavel would nod, but the words never fit him, not really.

He'd meant to go straight home after work, but his own legs betrayed him, steering him instead to the old tenement on Petrovska Street. He couldn't say why he went—he could have told himself he was only checking that she was all right, but he didn't like lying anymore, not even to himself. So he let his body move and didn't force his mind to keep up.

There was a faint light in the window. The glass was smeared with fingerprints, and as he squinted up at it, he could just make out a thin silhouette moving behind the dirty lace curtains. He stood there for a long time, his heart ticking faster, wondering whether to go up or walk away.

Someone bumped into him from behind. "Pavel! What are you doing standing out here like a street post?" Razumihin's voice was too loud for the quiet street. He grinned, an armful of groceries clutched to his chest, his hat askew. 

"I was just passing by," Pavel said, looking away.

"You want to see her," Razumihin replied, not bothering to lower his voice. "Why don't you go up, then?"

Pavel pressed his lips together. "I don't want to bother her."

Razumihin rolled his eyes. "You think too much. If you went up, maybe you'd actually know how she feels. Instead you stand out here in the cold and let your thoughts freeze you solid."

He started to say something, but a sharp sound from above interrupted him. The window rattled and then opened with a squeal. Anya leaned out, her shawl huddled around her shoulders, eyes bright in the gloom.

"Pavel? Is that you?"

He stepped back, suddenly embarrassed. "Yes. I was—just passing by."

She looked at him for a moment, then smiled. "You might as well come up. I've made some tea. Razumihin, you too!"

"See?" Razumihin muttered, nudging him. "It helps to be direct."

The climb up the stairs was steep, the banister slick with years of hands. Pavel followed Razumihin, the groceries shifting awkwardly between them. Anya held the door open, and the little room was suddenly full with the two of them. 

It was no different than before—patched chairs, the faint smell of old books and lemon peels, the quiet ticking of the clock. Anya poured tea, careful not to spill, her hands steady. 

"So, what brings you here?" she asked, settling back into her chair.

Pavel looked at her, then at his friend, uncertain. Razumihin filled the silence, talking about work, the too-early frost, his own misadventures. Anya laughed, her eyes crinkling, and the room felt warmer. But Pavel felt the words caught in his throat. He wanted to say something—anything—but everything seemed foolish on his tongue.

At last, Razumihin ran out of stories and stood to leave. "I should get going," he said, swinging his coat over his arm. "And Pavel, try not to stand outside in the cold next time. Grow a spine, my friend!" He winked at Anya, who shook her head, smiling.

When the door closed, the room was quieter. Anya cleared the cups and then sat across from Pavel, her hands folded in her lap. 

"Why did you come?" she asked softly.

He hesitated, unsure if honesty was bravery or folly. He watched the steam unravel from his cup.

"I suppose I wanted to see you," he managed. "To see if you were all right."

She didn't speak for a moment, then reached across the table, her hand resting next to his. "You could have just said that."

He felt foolish and relieved all at once. The city outside felt far away, the troubles a little smaller. They sat in silence, neither needing to fill it. For once, Pavel let the moment be,

Dear Clara,

I am writing this letter on the old wooden desk by the window, late in the evening. I think of you often and, as I write, I find myself wishing I could see your face in the flickering lamplight. So many things have happened since you left for the city two months ago, and I know it has been too long since my last letter. I suppose I am writing now because there is so much I want to tell you, and, though I do not have all the right words, I must try.

The days here are slower without your laughter in the house. The garden has changed almost overnight; the roses you planted have grown wild, sprawling across the fence as if trying to escape. Mother says the house feels emptier, though she wouldn’t admit it in so many words. I try to fill the silence with music, playing the old piano when the chores are done, but the notes seem to fall into a quiet that even music cannot reach.

I want you to know that I have read your last letter over and over. I keep it hidden in the drawer, away from sunlight and curious eyes. You wrote about the lessons you are taking, the city’s endless noise, and the crowded streets that never seem to sleep. You asked if I was lonely here, and I never answered truthfully. The truth is, I am a little lonely, but I have learned a kind of patience I did not know I possessed. It is as if I am waiting for something, though I do not know what.

You once said that knowing what you want is the most important lesson there is. I have thought about that a great deal. Some days I think I want to leave for the city and see the world as you do. Other days, I think I want only the quiet of home, the sound of the wind in the trees, and the comfort of ordinary things. I do not know which is truer. Perhaps both are, and I am meant to live between them for a while. I do know that, for now, I want to understand myself better, to listen for the small voice that tells me who I am. That is one lesson I wish you could teach me, though I suspect I must learn it alone.

Last Sunday, I went to church with Mother. The pews were half-empty, and the minister spoke about faith—how sometimes, when we cannot see the road ahead, we must trust that God is guiding us. I am not sure what I believe, but I do know the comfort of ritual: the way sunlight falls through stained glass, the warmth of hands joined in prayer, and the quiet moments after the last hymn, when everyone lingers before stepping back into the world. I wonder if you have found a church in the city or if you have left that behind, too, with so much else. I hope you have found something, or someone, to hold onto when the days grow long.

Father has grown quieter these past months. He asks about you, sometimes, but never says so directly. When the post arrives, he pretends not to notice whether a letter bears your handwriting. He spends more time in the fields, coming home late, hands stained with earth. I think he worries you will forget this place, but I know you better than that. You have always carried home with you, wherever you go.

I suppose I am writing not because I have answers, but because I have questions. I want to know if you are happy. I want to know if you sometimes wish you had stayed, or if your world is so wide you have forgotten how small ours can be. I want to know if the lessons you are learning are making you stronger, or if they are only making you tired. I want to know if you think of me, as I think of you, when the night is quiet and the city hushes for a moment.

Perhaps, in time, the answers will come. Until then, I will keep writing. I will tend the roses and play the piano. I will try to find joy in small things. And when you return—and I hope you do, even just for a while—I will be here, waiting by the window, ready to listen to all the stories you have brought back with you.

With love,

Anna

In the city of Athens, where the sun fell in golden sheets on pale stone, there lived a man named Timon. He was known to all, though few could truly claim to know him. His house stood apart from the others, at the edge of the olive groves, where the breeze from the hills carried the scent of thyme and dust. In his early days, Timon delighted in the company of friends. He opened his doors to all, feasted them, laughed with them, and called each man “brother.” There was no request he would deny, no jest he would not join.

But time is a wheel, and fortune rides upon it. When Timon’s wealth was spent, when his feasts grew rare and his laughter was tinged with worry, the city’s friends drifted away. He sent for one, then another, each with a reason for absence. Some wrote polite refusals; others gave none at all. A few, remembering past gifts, offered him only empty words and the dust of broken promises. Through it all, Timon waited at his gates, hoping each day for a change.

One afternoon, as the shadows lengthened, a stranger approached. He was a thin man, his tunic patched at the elbows, but he carried himself with a certain pride. “Art thou Timon of Athens?” he asked, voice steady.

Timon regarded him. “I am he. What dost thou seek at my door?”

The stranger bowed. “I seek not gold nor food, but a friend. I have heard stories of thy generosity. I have nothing to offer but my company.”

Timon’s lips curled in a wry smile. “Mayhap that is worth more than gold, in these days when old friends are cold and new friends are few. What is thy name?”

“Menander, son of Eudorus. I have come from the harbor. I saw thee once, in better days, when the city sang thy praises.”

Timon invited Menander inside. They sat beneath the vines, watching the evening come. Menander spoke of the sea, of trade and distant lands. Timon listened, one hand resting on the arm of his chair, the other tracing patterns in the dust. As twilight deepened, he found himself confiding in this new companion. He spoke of loss, of the bitterness that follows when one’s trust is betrayed. Menander listened, saying little. At last, Timon sighed.

“I have given much, and gained nothing. Is it the curse of Athens, that friends are fair in fortune and false in need?”

Menander shook his head. “Not all, Timon. Not all. There are those for whom friendship is more than a feast, who care not for thy purse but for thy company.”

Timon looked at him, searching for any hint of mockery. He found only sincerity.

The days passed. Menander returned, sometimes bringing bread or olives, sometimes nothing but stories. They walked the groves, speaking of philosophy and fate. Timon’s bitterness faded, though it did not vanish. He no longer awaited letters or knocks at the door. He no longer woke in the morning with hope, nor slept at night with disappointment. He let go of what was lost.

One night, as they sat by the fire, a letter arrived. The seal was familiar—an old friend, one who had once sworn eternal loyalty. Timon opened it with trembling hands. The words were polite, apologetic. The friend had heard of Timon’s troubles and wished to offer support—now, when there was little left to gain.

Timon laughed, a low sound that echoed in the small room. “See, Menander? When all is gone, the city remembers me. When the feasts are but memory, they write with fine words.”

Menander leaned forward. “Wilt thou accept his aid?”

Timon folded the letter. “Nay. I have learned, at last, to know my friends. Those who come not for gold, but for nothing, save a place by the fire.”

Menander smiled. “Then thou art richer now than in all thy days of plenty.”

Timon nodded, watching the flames dance. The night outside was very still. In the silence, two men sat together, and found that, sometimes, nothing is all a friend may bring—and all that thou may need.

The games were always announced with great ceremony, trumpets blaring from the city’s highest towers, banners unfurled along the avenues, and the people pressing into the squares as if to glimpse the gods themselves parading among mortals, yet beneath the spectacle and the laughter and the clatter of coins changing hands, Rian saw the same tightness in every jaw, the same wary flicker in their eyes, as though they all understood the truth but were afraid to name it aloud. For the games, though celebrated in public and sanctified by the Temple, were not merely a test of skill or luck, nor a harmless diversion to amuse the gods who, it was said, sometimes leaned from their seats in the sky to watch men contend for honor and survival; they were, in fact, a mechanism to sift the worthy from the wicked, and Rian, who had spent his childhood in the shadow of the arena, knew too well how thin the line could be between glory and condemnation.

It had always been this way, or so the elders insisted, telling stories as old as stone about the dawn of the city, when the gods, tired of chaos among mortals, decreed that every year on the eve of summer, the names of eight men and women would be drawn by lot from among the citizens and brought forth to play the games, their fates determined by a sequence of challenges so elaborate and capricious that not even the priests could claim to understand every rule or its purpose. Those who failed, who stumbled or balked or flinched at the wrong moment, were judged not simply as unlucky but as unworthy, their names struck from the city’s records and their families shunned for a generation. Those who won stood at the city’s heart in robes of crimson and gold, raised to heights they could never have imagined, their families honored, their children granted privileges beyond the reach of ordinary men.

But among the market stalls and in the quiet rooms behind shuttered windows, people whispered what could not be spoken in daylight: that sometimes the games were not fair, that the lots were drawn with a hidden hand, that the Temple’s favor could be bought or traded for a secret, that the gods themselves had grown indifferent or distracted by matters in the heavens and no longer watched as carefully as they once did. Rian had heard these whispers since childhood; his own father had vanished after his turn in the games, and though the official account named him a coward and a cheat, Rian’s mother had told him a different story, one that he kept locked behind his teeth, recited only in the silence of night when the city’s revels faded and the shadows pressed close.

Now, with his name drawn for the first time, Rian felt the weight of both legacies—the public one, full of expectation and pride, and the secret one, tangled with loss and suspicion—settle on his shoulders as he moved through the city toward the arena. The streets were lined with faces he knew, friends and rivals alike, all transformed by the knowledge that one of their own would stand before the gods and the judges. Some called out encouragements, a few made signs of protection, and still others averted their eyes as he passed, unwilling to gamble their own fortunes by associating too closely with one marked by fate.

Inside the arena, the sun was blinding, glinting off marble and gold, and the crowd’s roar echoed up into the pale blue sky. The other chosen men and women stood beside him, faces set in expressions of grim determination or barely contained fear. The High Priest, swathed in ceremonial white, recited the invocation, calling on the gods to observe and judge, and then the first of the games began: a test of memory and precision, in which each contestant was required to recall the sequence of ancient laws spoken by the priest and to inscribe them in the sand without error.

Rian’s hands trembled as he knelt, the memory of his father’s last words flickering at the edge of his thoughts, but he forced himself to focus, to push away the noise, the heat, the eyes of the city upon him. He remembered the stories his mother had whispered, the secret code she claimed was hidden in the words, something only the worthy could see, and as he traced the symbols into the sand, he felt for the first time a strange certainty, as if someone were guiding his hand. The judges watched, the crowd held its breath, and as Rian finished, he looked up, not at the priests or the people, but at the patch of empty sky where, if the old tales were true, the gods might still be watching, waiting to see which of the wicked would be revealed, and which could be counted among the worthy.

The process of making dough may seem straightforward, but when precision is required, every gram and every minute matters. Measuring exactly 250 grams of flour and combining it with water at the right temperature requires both patience and accuracy, especially when you are trying to halve a recipe or adjust quantities for a smaller batch. The speed at which you mix the ingredients also plays a crucial role in the final texture; kneading too quickly or slowly can affect gluten development. Setting a timer for eight minutes and following a clear diagram of the kneading steps helps ensure that the dough achieves the perfect elasticity needed for baking. Paying attention to these details, even something as small as folding the dough at intervals, can make a significant difference in the end result. In baking, discipline with measurements and timing transforms simple ingredients into something extraordinary.

When considering the variation in climate between different Australian cities, it is fascinating to reflect on the daily experience of winter. For instance, the average maximum temperature in Brisbane during July is notably higher than that of Canberra, which makes a considerable difference in how residents and visitors perceive the season. In Brisbane, July days tend to be mild and pleasant, with average maximums reaching into the low twenties in degrees Celsius. People can often be seen walking along the riverfront in light jackets, enjoying outdoor cafes, and making the most of the gentle winter sun. In contrast, Canberra’s winter is far sharper. The daily maximum in July hovers several degrees lower, frequently struggling to reach double digits. Frosty mornings are common, and the cold persists well into the afternoon. Residents adapt by layering their clothing, seeking warmth indoors, and perhaps even appreciating the cozy atmosphere that the chilly air provides. These differences underscore not just the diversity of Australian climates but also the ways in which daily life adjusts to the weather. Whether one prefers the mild, sunny days of Brisbane or the crisp, invigorating air of Canberra, the character of July is shaped as much by temperature averages as by the routines and attitudes of the people who live through them.

Food consumption around the world varies greatly, shaped by tradition, geography, and economic conditions. Rice, for example, is the staple in Cambodia, forming the foundation of every meal. Families may eat rice three times a day, and the average calorie intake per person from rice is incredibly high. In contrast, maize holds a similar status in Mexico, where it is used in tortillas, snacks, and drinks. For Mexicans, maize is not just a source of calories; it is intertwined with national identity. In Egypt, bread made from wheat is a dietary constant, supplying a large share of daily energy. Meanwhile, Poland’s cuisine highlights potatoes and bread, though the calorie intake per capita is often supplemented by dairy and meat. These regional differences demonstrate that the way people meet their basic nutritional needs is deeply cultural. Whether through rice, maize, or wheat, societies adapt crops to climate and history, making food not just sustenance, but also a symbol of identity and belonging.

Ethanol production from corn has become an important process in the search for renewable fuels. The journey from raw corn to usable ethanol involves several steps, each critical to the final product. The process begins with milling the corn to create a fine meal, which is then mixed with water and heated. This cooking stage, which might last several hours, helps break down the starches in the corn so that they can be more easily converted to sugars. Once cooled, enzymes are added to convert the starch into simple sugars, and yeast is introduced to begin fermentation. Over the next forty-eight hours or more, the yeast transforms the sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide. After fermentation, the mixture is distilled, separating the ethanol from the residual water and solids. Each point in this sequence, from grinding to distillation, requires close monitoring to ensure maximum efficiency. Ultimately, this careful process yields ethanol, a fuel that can help reduce our dependence on fossil energy sources.

Okay, so, honestly, I never really liked talking about my father. Not because he was some monster or whatever, but because, well, how do you talk about someone who feels like a ghost most of the time? I guess that's the thing about fathers—they're either too much right in your face, or they're barely there at all, just a shadow, you know? So you end up filling in all the blanks with stories you half-remember, or stuff your mother says when she’s tipsy and angry at the sink.

But, alright, this isn’t about her. This is about me and my brother, and, yeah, my father—Sir Robert. Well, not like "sir" like he got knighted or anything, more like everyone just called him Sir Robert because he’d walk around acting like he owned the place. And sometimes, in a way, he kind of did. He owned the land our house was on, a couple acres of rough, stubborn grass and some apple trees that never really bore much fruit. You could stand at the edge and see all the way to the river on a clear day, not that it was ever that clear.

My brother, Dan, was always saying how one day he’d be the one telling people what to do, not Sir Robert. He’d lift his chin and try to look older, and I’d laugh and say, "Sure, when pigs fly," and he’d get all red. Thing is, Dan was the proper son, at least in our father’s eyes. The sort of kid that always came home with his hair combed and his shirt tucked in. I was—well, let's just say, my mother sometimes used the word "bastard" when she was mad, and not always in a joking way.

It’s weird, how a word can hang in the air like smoke. You don’t want to breathe it in, but you do, and you can’t get it out again after. Sir Robert never called me that, at least not to my face, but he didn’t have to. There’s a way a man looks at someone that says everything, and it’s worse than any word.

So one summer, I was maybe fifteen, Dan seventeen, and Sir Robert started talking about the land. He’d sit out back in that old, cracked chair, drinking his beer, watching the sunset, and he’d say, “One day, all this is yours, Dan. You've got to keep it right, keep it in the family.” I’d be standing right there, but it's like I was invisible, like I was the wind messing up the grass.

Does it make sense to want something just because someone says you can’t have it? I never cared about the land, not really, but suddenly it turned important. I started spending more time outside, walking the edge of the property, picking up rocks, throwing them at the fence. I mean, who was I, really? The spare? The secret? Like, what would happen to me when Sir Robert died? Would I just disappear, like he always seemed to hope I would?

One night, Dan found me sitting by the old barn. He plopped down next to me, didn’t say much at first, just picked at the dirt. After a long while, he goes, “He’s just scared. That’s why he acts like that.” I stared at him, confused, because I’d always thought Sir Robert was too tough for fear, you know? Dan shrugged, kicking a pebble. “He’s scared I’ll mess it up. Maybe he’s scared you’ll want it so bad, you’ll take it.”

And I laughed, but I could feel something shift between us. Brothers, but not really—never quite equal. He was born right; I was a stray, a maybe. Still, we sat there, shoulder to shoulder, and for a second, it didn’t matter who’d get the land or who was whose son.

Here’s what I think: families are weird as hell. Who gets to count, who doesn’t. Do we stay because of love, or just because it’s what we know? It’s messy and unfair and sometimes it makes you want to run far away and never look back.

But, you know, next morning I woke up early, grabbed two apples—sour as ever—and tossed one to Dan. He caught it, smiled, and for just a moment, we were both just kids again. Not sons of Sir Robert, not “proper” or “bastard,” just two brothers, with the whole stubborn, scraggly land stretching out behind us, and the sun coming up like maybe today things could be different.

So you wanna hear about Warwick, right? I mean, the thing is, not many folks know the whole deal. Edward, Richard, and all that mess—there's a lot to unpack, honestly. You ever wonder why people get so fired up about blood and right? Like, who gets to be king and who should, and why does it matter so much? Sometimes I think it's all just tradition, but then you see how they, uh, actually fought each other over it—you know, swords and all.

Warwick, yeah, he was always in the thick of it. Not that he wanted it, I guess, but thou canst hardly blame him, given how things stood. If I recall, Edward was kinda the favorite for a while, but Richard, well, he was the younger one, wasn’t he? Right blood, maybe. Or just lucky, depending on how you see it. Look, the thing is, everyone said Warwick had power, but what’s power anyway? Is it just money, soldiers, or—um—something else entirely?

Thy neighbor might tell thee Warwick betrayed Edward, but it wasn’t that simple. I mean, honestly, people switch sides all the time, don’t they? Sometimes for love, sometimes for, uh, survival. Some said Warwick was only after his own interests, but who isn’t, right? And then, when Warwick backed Edward, things looked up for a while. But then Edward started acting all kingly and didn’t listen quite enough, so Warwick’s like, nah, I’m out.

And Richard, he was always in the shadow—like, the little brother. People kinda ignored him, but he was clever. You ever notice how the quiet ones often end up coming out on top? Guess that’s just how it goes. Anyway, Edward got made king, but Warwick wasn’t happy. He didn’t feel like he got the right share, or maybe he thought Edward owed him more than thanks. So he started looking elsewhere. Some folks say Warwick was a schemer, but I dunno, that sounds harsh. Everyone schemes if the stakes are high enough.

Okay, let's back up. Edward had, uh, the right blood, technically, but that doesn’t mean everyone accepted him. There were whispers—like, maybe he wasn’t really the rightful king. Or maybe someone else had a better claim. People always chasing after something, and honestly, no one’s ever fully satisfied, right? Like, you get the throne and then find out it’s more trouble than it’s worth.

When Warwick turned on Edward—that’s the wild part. Do you think loyalty’s real, or is it just what people say to sound noble? He threw his support behind another claimant, and suddenly the whole country was in chaos. Battles, shifting alliances, all that. And Richard? I mean, he watched everything, biding his time. Sometimes I wonder how he felt, seeing his brothers and friends fighting for something so messy.

Thou knowest, if there’s one thing clear—it’s that blood and the right to rule mean less than, uh, people think. I mean, you can have royal ancestors and still be nobody if the wrong folks decide it. Did Warwick regret it, after everything? Maybe, maybe not. He died in battle eventually, and that’s just how these things end, isn’t it? People chase after crowns, lose friends, and sometimes all they get is a grave.

Edward kept the throne, but lost some trust. Richard learned from all of it, I reckon. Maybe that’s why he ended up so, uh, careful later on. There's a lesson in there somewhere, I guess. Is it that blood doesn’t matter? Or that you gotta be smart? Honestly, I’m not sure. You see all these old stories, and think, maybe they could've just talked it out instead of fighting. But I guess that's not how things work when pride and, well, crown are at stake.

Anyway, that’s Warwick, Edward, Richard—the kings and the almost-kings. It’s messy. You can be born with the right blood and still lose everything, or you can start from nowhere and end up ruling, if you play it right. Sometimes it’s luck, sometimes it’s timing, and, uh, sometimes folks just don’t know when to quit. That's kinda the point, isn't it? Would you pick loyalty or ambition? Or maybe just peace, if that was even possible back then. I dunno. It’s a lot to think about, really.

So, right, Titus is scrubbing his face in a cracked mirror and there's greasepaint everywhere—on the towel, on his collar, and even smudged on the edge of the sink. It's like, how much face do you need for one sad clown? Apparently, way more than you think. The circus tent outside is all faded stripes, sagging a little, and pigeons are stomping around in the dirt, like they're waiting for their own cue to waddle out under the big spotlight. 

"Sir, you—uh, sir, they're, um, they're calling for you," says some kid, can't be older than ten, probably a cousin of the ringmaster. Titus waves at him, not even turning, 'cause he's got most of a bright red lip left to fix. It's a ridiculous thing, honestly, to worry about makeup when the tent's not even a quarter full. Still, a clown's got to look like a clown.

I mean, the thing is, folks come for the Emperor. That's what they call old Titus in the lineup—"His Mad Majesty, the Emperor of Laughter," which is... eh, it's a stretch. He's just a man in baggy pants that don't fit right anymore. When did those pants start shrinking? Or is it just him getting bigger? Or, you know, maybe the world just wants everyone to play pretend. Who even knows?

The air's thick with the smell of popcorn and damp straw, and you can hear the pigeons cooing, flapping around the rafters, even from inside the dressing tent. He sighs, grabs his battered crown—a sparkly thing made of tin and cheap glass—and squints at himself. He pulls a face, big wide eyes, sticks his tongue out. There, that's the Emperor. Or at least it's something.

He shuffles out, nearly tripping over the edge of the rug—seriously, why's it always bunched up in the same spot?—and the ringmaster's bellowing about wonders untold, marvels never before seen. It's a good speech, gets folks sitting up straight, but Titus' bit comes after the strongman and before that girl with the fire hula hoops, so most people are in the mood for a laugh but too busy checking their phones or elbowing each other to really pay attention.

When he steps into the light, the pigeons flutter up, and one nearly whacks him with its wing. He almost breaks character right there, but instead, he turns it into a pratfall. Drops the prop scepter, falls flat on his butt, and the kids all giggle, which is... well, that's the point, isn't it?

"Thou art a scoundrel!" he yells, pointing at a pigeon that’s strutting around like it owns the ring. Plays it up with his best fake Shakespearean, which gets a laugh from some older folks, but a groan from the ringmaster in the wings. Guess it's not in the script. 

Honestly, the best part is just making it up. You get these moments where you forget everyone's watching. It's like, you become somebody else. Somebody who can talk to pigeons and make them villains, and the scepter's a legendary sword, and the emperor's crown isn't just a hat that's too small. Everything's magic, or at least, it feels like it for five minutes.

He juggles rubber chickens, trips over a bucket, and when he bows, a pigeon lands on his head, and—no joke—just stays there, pecking curiously at his tin crown. The crowd bursts out laughing and he grins, and it's one of those real grins, you know? The kind that sticks around even after you've left the ring.

But after, in the little alley behind the tent, he peels off the crown and the paint and stands there in the dusk. Shoots a glance up at the pigeons on the wires—they look like lumpy little statues. He wonders, just for a second, if they’re waiting for the next act, or if they even care at all. Do they remember any of it? Do the kids? 

The thing is, you never really know. Maybe tomorrow, someone’ll tell him he was funny, or maybe they’ll just remember the pigeons. And that's okay. It's all just part of the job. 

He shakes out his boots, picks up the crown, and heads back in. There's another show in an hour, and the Emperor—well, he shall return, whether the tent’s full or not. That's the only thing he can promise.

So, I guess, if you want to know how it all started, you'd probably need to picture this rickety old apartment, cracked yellow walls, and this shambling little sofa with springs that groan every time you move. Marfa was sitting there hunched—she always hunched, I swear—sucking on the tail end of a cigarette and peering out at nothing, really. If you asked her, she’d say she was watching for birds, but I never saw a single one in all the months I lived there. Just dust and, sometimes, scraps of paper the wind tossed around the street.

The thing is, everybody said Marfa Petrovna was… how do you put it? A force. That’s the word they’d use, but it’s not what you’d expect. She wasn’t the loud, bustling kind of force, more like a stubborn tree root that splits the pavement, y’know? She had this way of making you feel like you were both invisible and, at the same time, completely scrutinized. I don’t know if that makes sense. Maybe it does if you ever met someone like that.

And Avdotya Romanovna—well, she was nothing like Marfa, at least at first glance. Picture her in her red scarf, always knotted loosely, with this energy, like she was always ready to step into the next scene, wherever that was. There was this rumor—okay, maybe not a rumor, but people talked—that she’d be the first woman in the block to go to university, but who can really keep track of this stuff? Anyway, even if it was just a story, it stuck to her, same way the dust stuck to her shoes.

I guess, looking back, you could say the shape of things between them was always shifting. People love to talk about love, right? But I’m not sure anyone really knows what they mean. For Marfa, it was like, I dunno, she felt things so heavy that she could barely look at Avdotya sometimes. She’d start to say something meaningful—something that, if you wrote it down, might even sound profound—but words would get lost somewhere in her chest. That’s the thing with love, isn’t it? It doesn’t always come out the way you wish it would. And honestly, sometimes it doesn’t come out at all.

One night, I remember, Marfa was pacing. The floors creaked, and the lamp on the little table quivered with each step. She kept muttering to herself—stuff about fate and luck and how life isn’t fair and all that. Avdotya just sat there, her legs curled under her, reading some battered old novel. She didn’t look up until Marfa stopped right behind her. There was this silence that felt thick, like you could touch it, but nobody said anything for a minute.

Then, out of nowhere, Marfa just blurted, “Would you—do you think you could, I mean, would you ever…?” And she trailed off, obviously terrified she’d said too much or not enough. In that way, I think she was braver than anyone else I knew. Sometimes the bravest thing is to fumble through, right? Who cares if you sound foolish?

Avdotya, she just laughed a little, but not meanly. She closed her book, set it aside, and, you know, for a second she looked almost shy, which was rare for her. She said, “I don’t know what I would do. I just know I want to be here right now.” And that was it. Just those words, but it changed something, I think. It changed Marfa, for sure. Maybe Avdotya too.

But here’s the catch—life didn’t get suddenly magical. They still argued about whether to leave the window open at night, and still forgot to buy tomatoes at the market, and Marfa’s old cat still brought in dead sparrows. The streets outside stayed loud and ugly, and the future didn’t get any less uncertain. But, you know, sometimes Marfa would look at Avdotya and forget, just for a second, all the things she was scared of. She’d smile, a real odd, crooked kind of smile, and Avdotya would notice. They kept going, even if nobody else understood why.

So, is that love? Or is it just two people being stubborn enough not to walk away? And does it matter, really? I don’t think I have the answer. Maybe nobody does. Maybe that’s the point.

So, like, here's the thing about Antony—it was impossible not to notice him. I mean, he walked into the room like he owned it, and honestly, maybe he did, in some way or another. Everyone would just sort of look up and pretend they weren't paying attention, but you could feel it. People talk about charisma and all that, but what does that even mean? It's like, he's got this energy, but you can't put your finger on it.

And Enobarbus, he'd always be right there, not quite in the spotlight but close enough. He had this grin, sly and kind at the same time. If you tried to figure him out, you'd just end up spinning your wheels. It's not like he was hiding things, but he sorta gave you the feeling that he knew more about the world than he let on. Was he loyal? I guess, but loyalty's weird, isn't it? Like, what even counts as loyalty when you're hanging out with the queen herself?

Cleopatra, oh, wow. Let me tell you, I don't really know how she did it. One minute, she's laughing, the next she's dead serious, and after that she's all soft and whispery. You're left standing there wondering if you said something wrong. People told stories about her—some you couldn't believe, others sounded too true. She wasn't just the queen, she was the idea of the queen. And if you ever saw her, you'd get why folks would follow her anywhere. Scarus told me once, after he'd had a bit too much, that she could make you feel like you mattered, even if all you did was carry armor or clean up after the horses.

Sometimes Eros would come in, usually without much fuss. He'd stand against the wall, arms crossed, watching everything. Not many people talked to him, but Antony did. If Antony asked him for anything, Eros would just nod and get to it. No big speeches, just action. Maybe that's what made him different; he wasn't flashy, but you could count on him.

Now, Scarus was rough around the edges. I'm not saying he was rude, just that he didn't care much for manners. He'd walk right up to you and ask what you were doing, and if you tried to lie, he'd roll his eyes and wander off. Sometimes he'd joke about the old days, about how he got the scars on his arms and face. Once, he told me, "I got these from following fools," but he laughed right after, so maybe he meant it or maybe he didn't.

There was this day, kind of like any other, except you could feel something was off. The palace felt quieter, like everyone was holding their breath. Cleopatra sat with Antony by the window. The sunlight made her jewels glow, but she didn't say much. Enobarbus came in and tried to crack a joke, but nobody laughed. Eros was in the corner, as usual, and Scarus pretended to polish his sword but kept watching the sky.

Antony leaned over, murmured something to Cleopatra, and she looked away. That's the thing about them—they always seemed close, but there was this space you couldn't cross. What does it mean to love someone like that? To be so tied up in politics and power and danger that you barely know where your feelings end and your duty begins?

Later, Enobarbus found me outside, where the garden was empty. He just sighed and said, "It's all coming apart, isn't it?" And, honestly, I didn't know how to answer. I wanted to say it'd be fine, that things always work out, but I couldn't make myself believe it. The thing is, when people like Antony and Cleopatra start looking worried, you know something's about to go wrong.

Night came and the air seemed thick. There were voices in the hall, whispering—Scarus, Eros, a couple others. Everyone wanted to know what was next, but nobody knew. Cleopatra went to her rooms and closed the door. Antony drank and paced. Enobarbus stayed near the balcony, eyes searching for something out in the dark.

I guess the real question is, does it matter how brave you are if the world decides not to go your way? And if you get a chance to stand next to someone like the queen, would you take it, even if it meant losing everything else? People make choices, and sometimes those choices make them. Maybe that's just how it goes.

Cordelia was sitting on the porch steps, tying her shoes for what seemed like the thousandth time that morning. The sky was a flat gray—no drama, just that boring blanket you see when the weather can’t make up its mind. She paused, looking out across the yard. Did she actually love this place, or was it just that she’d always been here? Honestly, the answer changed depending on the day.

Her dad, Lear, came out with his coffee and a newspaper tucked under his arm, humming some tune he probably made up. “Ready to go yet, Cordelia?” he asked, but his voice had that edge, like he didn’t care whether she was ready or not.

“Yeah, almost,” she mumbled, trying to remember what she was supposed to say. There was a thing about speaking up—her uncle Gloucester always said you should speak your mind but, the thing is, she never really knew how much was too much. Saying nothing sometimes seemed easier.

Lear watched her for a moment, then said, “You should say what you feel. Otherwise folks’ll just walk all over you. Lord knows I learned that the hard way.” He sipped his coffee, eyes going distant like he was seeing something nobody else saw.

Cordelia wanted to ask what he meant, but honestly, she wasn’t sure he’d answer. Or if he did, it’d be a whole story about the time he lost his wallet or missed a job interview. Her dad’s stories always started somewhere and ended nowhere. Was everybody’s memory like that, or was it just men of a certain age? She decided not to ask.

“Don’t forget your bag,” Lear said, but he didn’t help her pick it up. She slung it over her shoulder and tried to smile, but the thing is, her mouth wasn’t cooperating. Gloucester drove up then—his truck rattling louder than usual.

“Morning, Cordelia! Morning, Lear!” Gloucester yelled, getting out and nearly tripping over his own feet. “You two ready to roll?”

Cordelia nodded, even though nothing felt ready, not her shoes, not her bag, not her head. They piled into the truck, and Gloucester started talking before anyone could get a word in. “You know, love’s not just about saying the right thing. Sometimes it’s about saying nothing at all. People get so hung up on words, but silence says plenty.”

Lear grunted. “Silence says nothing, if you ask me.” He glanced at Cordelia. “What do you think?”

Cordelia looked out the window, watching the trees whip past. She wanted to say, I don’t know. She wanted to say, I don’t have anything to add. She ended up saying, “Sometimes I just don’t know what to say.”

Gloucester gave a big laugh. “That’s honest, kid. That’s more than most folks manage.”

The ride dragged on. Lear read his paper, muttering about politics and the price of eggs. Gloucester drove, humming as he went. Cordelia felt like she was floating, a passenger in her own life. Do you ever wonder if you’re just repeating the same mistakes over and over? She did, but she kept it to herself.

Later, at the lake, Lear sat on a bench and let the sun warm his face. Gloucester skipped rocks, missing more than he hit. Cordelia took her shoes off and dipped her toes in the water, watching the ripples stretch and fade.

After a while, Lear spoke up, not looking at her. “You know, if you never speak, nobody knows what you want. Lord knows I’ve been guilty of that. I’d just let things pass—let people decide for me.”

Cordelia answered softly, “But saying nothing feels safer. Like, if I don’t say anything, I can’t get it wrong.”

Gloucester tossed a rock, shaking his head. “You’re young. You’ll find your voice, and when you do, it’ll surprise you.”

Silence settled around them, not uncomfortable, but full of questions nobody had the words for yet. Cordelia looked at her dad and then at Gloucester, and thought about what love meant. Was it about speaking up, or was it the quiet sitting together by the water, letting the world be what it was, just for a moment?

Her hair blew in her eyes, and she pushed it back. Maybe she didn’t need answers right now. Maybe nothing was fine.

So, the thing is, I guess, when you wake up and it’s one of those heavy, gray mornings where the world feels like it’s been put on mute and the sky can’t even be bothered to look blue anymore, you get this weird itch to find some kind of pleasure, or—well, you know, I don’t mean anything fancy, just something, anything to take the edge off. I remember one such morning, lying there on my back, listening to the old fridge groan like it was just as tired as me, thinking, “Is this all there is for today?” But then, I don’t know, I think I realized something, or at least I started hoping I did, which is probably just as good—maybe better, actually, ’cause hoping almost feels like pleasure, too, or at least like a promise you gave yourself that you’re not totally lost.

I mean, people talk a lot about glory, don’t they? Like it’s this shining, solid thing sitting up on a shelf, waiting for the right person to come along and claim it, but honestly, who’s actually seen it up close? I sure haven’t, and I’d bet most folks haven’t either, though they’d probably pretend otherwise if you asked. I think glory’s sort of like one of those things you keep chasing, but even if you catch up, it kind of slips through your hands the second you try to hold on tight—like water, like smoke, or maybe like nothing at all, which is kind of irritating and, well, sort of a relief too if I’m being honest.

Sometimes I wonder, though, if we’re not just making up needs and reasons for things, just so we can feel like we have some control over them. Like, does pleasure mean anything by itself, or is it—uh, is it only a thing because we decided it should be? I guess what I’m trying to say is that sometimes, chasing after pleasure just ends up making me more tired than I was before, like maybe the chase is the whole point, and the second you stop, you’re forced to sit with yourself and your boredom or sadness or whatever, and that’s, uh, that’s hard. Maybe we cling to things that make us feel one way or another just to avoid feeling nothing at all—I know I do, anyway.

And there’s this other thing—I don’t know if this’ll make sense—when you want to please someone, it’s not always about them, is it? I mean, you tell yourself it is, but honestly, it’s so you can look at yourself in the mirror and say, “Hey, you did good. You made someone smile,” and that’s supposed to patch the day together. But, I mean, what happens when pleasing others starts to feel empty, or like, you know, more work than it’s worth? And what if there are days where nothing seems to click, no matter how hard you try—what are you supposed to do then?

Like, let me try and explain—there was this one time, not long ago, where I tried and tried to cheer up my friend, but everything felt forced, all the jokes fell flat, and it got awkward fast. I felt like I was performing on a stage with no spotlight and nobody in the seats. I kept thinking, “Why can’t I make this right?” but the harder I tried, the worse it got, until finally we just gave up and sat in silence eating chips, which, honestly, felt better than anything else I’d managed all day. Is that weird? I don’t know. Maybe that’s how things go sometimes—the more you push for some kind of shining moment, the more you realize maybe it’s not about glory at all, or pleasure, or making things perfect, but just being there when nothing is happening.

And yeah, maybe that doesn’t sound like much, and maybe it won’t ever be written about in a book or sung in some song about heroes, but sometimes, just sitting with someone, wishing things could be better but not pretending they are, feels like the best thing you can do. Who made the rules for what counts as glory anyway? Maybe some days, it’s just keeping your head above water, or sharing a bag of chips in silence, and not needing anything more than that.

Honestly, I keep thinking about what happened that afternoon, the one where Lydia came storming into the house, all noise and wild stories, and the whole mood sort of... shifted, I guess. You know how it is when someone just pushes through the front door like a gust of wind, and for a second, nobody’s sure what’s going on? So, anyway, Lydia was always like that. She’d throw her bonnet onto the hall table, shoes half-untied, and tell us she’d seen something—usually something that turned out a little exaggerated, but you couldn’t help but listen.

Elizabeth was reading by the window, and she had this look, like she’d been right in the middle of some thought, probably about… well, who knows? She was always thinking about all sorts of things, not that she ever really said much about it. The thing is, Lizzy would sometimes let you see these little smiles, like she knew something you didn’t. I’d ask her about it, but she’d just shrug, and it was impossible to tell if she was teasing or just didn't want to talk.

Anyway, Lydia barely made it inside before she started talking a mile a minute. “You won’t believe who I saw in town,” she said, barely stopping to breathe. “And they said—oh, Mama, you’ll never believe it!” Mrs. Bennet was in the kitchen, probably fussing with some potatoes or something, and as soon as she heard Lydia’s voice, you could hear her footsteps coming—quick, anxious, like she already expected trouble.

What always got me about our house was how fast things could go from quiet to chaos. One second, Kitty’s doodling flowers on the edge of some letter, Mary’s trying to pretend she’s too busy for us, and the next, everyone’s crowded around the hall trying to get the first bit of news. And, I mean, have you ever wondered why news from town always feels more important than it probably is? Maybe it’s because we just want something to shake up the day.

Lizzy stayed by the window for a minute, but it’s not like she could ignore Lydia—nobody could, really. Finally she set her book aside, and with this little sigh (not a loud one, just enough that I noticed), she got up and joined the rest of us. Kitty, as usual, was already bouncing from foot to foot, half-laughing, half-worried Lydia was about to say something embarrassing. Not that Kitty was really in a position to judge.

“Oh, come now, tell us properly,” Mrs. Bennet said, trying to sound patient but already red-cheeked. Lydia just grinned, and honestly, I don’t even remember what the news was. It was something about officers and dances, and the way she told it, it sounded like the world was about to change. But, you know, that’s how Lydia saw things. It’s sort of charming, when you think about it, or maybe just exhausting.

The thing about home is—actually, just, you know, thinking about it—I don’t think any of us realized how easy everything felt, even when we thought it was complicated. I mean, Mrs. Bennet would fuss and worry about the neighbors and who was courting who, but in the end, dinner was always on the table, and we all ended up together in one room, one way or another. Sometimes I wonder if that’s what matters, more than all the news and drama that came flying through the front door.

So, there was this moment, right after Lydia finished (or maybe just paused for breath), where everyone kind of... settled. Mary muttered something about propriety; Kitty giggled. Mrs. Bennet looked relieved, probably because nobody had eloped yet. And Lizzy, she just stood there, a little apart, her eyes flicking from Lydia to the window, like she was thinking about outside things even while she smiled at us.

Isn’t it funny how the house can feel so small and so big at the same time? Like, when it’s just you and your thoughts, every creak in the floorboards feels enormous, but when everyone’s there—talking and laughing and filling up all the space—it’s like you could live in those moments forever. I don’t know. Maybe that’s just the way home is supposed to feel.

And, look, I’m not going to pretend everything was perfect, because it wasn’t. We argued, doors got slammed, secrets were definitely kept, and I’m sure we all got sick of each other now and then. You know, life doesn’t really unfold like you expect—it kinda comes at you sideways, and I guess that’s something you figure out early if you’re paying attention, which I mostly wasn’t, what with growing up in a town that people just sorta forgot existed after the railroad pulled out. And, the thing is, I thought everybody’s father acted like Mapple did, always standing in the backyard with one hand gripping the fence like the wood was gonna float away if he blinked. I don’t even remember when people started calling him Mapple instead of his given name, but it just stuck, like a burr on old wool socks, and so we just rolled with it, ‘cause why make a fuss? 

Anyway, Mapple just had this way about him—he’d star at the sky most nights, which was weird, except he’d be muttering about the stars and how they’d never point you the same way twice and how, if you listened, you could feel which way was north just by breathing in real slow. I’d laugh at that, sometimes, but not to his face. And, honestly, the more I think about it, the more I wonder if that’s not what he meant about living, like, you just pick a direction, trust it for a while, and try not to get angry when it turns you someplace you didn’t expect. That said, when’s the last time you trusted your gut about anything bigger than lunch, huh? 

So, yeah, Mapple wasn’t much for giving advice directly. He was—you know—one of those guys who’d spend hours fixing the same loose shutter on the house, all the while humming a song you couldn’t quite catch, and you’d ask him what he was humming, and he’d shrug and say, “Just something old,” like that was a good enough answer. Maybe it was. Some days I’d sit next to him, pretending to help but mostly just looking out at the grass, trying to spot shapes in the clover, and he’d say, “You see that tree over there? That one with the two branches like it’s holding something?” and I’d nod, ‘cause it did look like that—like it was cradling something invisible—and he’d say, “That tree’s older than anything in this yard. My old man planted it, and I figure, if a thing’s been living that long, it probably knows more about sticking around than I do.” That kinda stuck with me, you know? How could it not? 

There was this old paper map we used to keep in the junk drawer in the kitchen, all creased and smudged from coffee stains and greasy fingerprints, never got thrown out even when Mom did her yearly “throw out what we don’t need” campaign. Mapple’d pull it out every couple of months, spread it across the kitchen table, and trace his finger across the faded lines—never with any urgency or reason, just to do it, like keeping up with old friends. “You think,” he’d say, with this odd look in his eye, “that life could be charted out on something like this? Or is it just random squiggles, somebody else’s idea of where things should go?” I’d laugh, but I never really knew how to answer. Do you? 

Oh, and—wait, let me back up a bit—when I was a kid, we used to have this neighbor, Mrs. Lambert, who’d say things like, “You can always tell what a man’s living for by watching the way he walks home at night.” I didn’t get it at the time, thought it was just one of those weird old people sayings, but now I kinda do. Now I’m older—well, older than I was, anyway—and sometimes I catch myself staring at the sky, trying to figure out if there’s a pattern to the stars that’ll tell me something useful. Spoiler: there isn’t, or maybe I’m just not tuned in right. But every so often, I’ll reach for that old map, even though the town’s changed, and roads’ve been built over or faded out, and I’ll trace my own finger along the crumpled edge, thinking, maybe Mapple was right. I mean, he wasn't lazy, but he had these wild ideas about luck, like the universe would just hand him a bag of gold if he asked nicely or something.

Tommy had this run-down apartment above a bakery that always smelled like burnt bread, which was either comforting or annoying, depending on the day. So, Tommy, right, he’d tell all his friends that someday he’d find this lost treasure—he didn’t really have a plan, but he talked about it like it was a sure thing. Now, I’m not saying he was wrong, but the thing is, while Tommy was busy dreaming, his own stuff kinda started multiplying. Shelves bowing, boxes stacked high, like he couldn’t let go of anything, as if all these lost possessions might add up to something big if he just waited long enough.

There was this one night, though, when a storm knocked out the power for pretty much the whole block. So, look, there's this story I keep thinking about—don’t ask me why, it just sticks in my mind like gum on a shoe. Orlando, you know, the tall guy with the wild hair, always messing around with that battered notebook of his? He’s, uh—well, he was standing in the park, or maybe it was a garden, but it doesn’t really matter, because the sun was in his eyes and he couldn’t see much anyhow. He keeps squinting, scribbling half-words, and mouthing sentences to himself like he’s trying to out-talk the wind. I asked him once, like, “Orlando, what’re you always writing?” and he just grinned at me, said, “Secrets, Celia, only for those who listen closely.” What does that even mean? I dunno, but it sounded important, so I laughed and let him have his mystery.

Celia—well, that’s me—and Rosalind, my cousin, we’d sit on that crooked bench near the old willow, trying to guess what Orlando’s deal was. Rosalind had this way of making everything seem like an adventure, even if we were just chasing dragonflies across a muddy field. “He’s in love,” she’d say, and honestly, I think she wanted it to be true, just for the story of it. “With his notebook?” I’d joke, but she always gave me that look, like I was missing something really obvious.

And then there’s Jaques. He’s—uh, he’s a bit harder to pin down. He’d wander in from nowhere, hands in his pockets, mouth twisted in this kind of half-smile. He always had something smart to say, but it’d sneak up on you, you know? You’d be talking about clouds or, uh, the taste of blackberries, and then he’d just go, “Why do we say ‘thou’ when we really mean ourselves?” Like, what? Who thinks like that? But he’d do it with such a straight face, you couldn’t tell if he was joking or not.

But the thing is, even with all his weird questions, Jaques sort of pressed all of us to look at things sideways. Once, he challenged Orlando—said, “Man, if thou art so clever, tell me what’s in thy heart.” Orlando got real quiet, fiddled with his pen, and Rosalind just burst out laughing. “You’d need more than a mouth to answer that,” she said, and I think we all agreed, though none of us really said so aloud.

Anyway, days passed in that kind of lazy, golden way they do when you’re not really waiting for anything to happen. Orlando kept showing up, always with another crumpled page, sometimes reading us bits if we pestered him, but mostly he’d mutter and stare at the clouds. Sometimes, when there was nothing else to do, we’d argue about words—why say ‘thou’ or ‘thy’ when ‘you’ would do just fine? Jaques had a ton of theories, but Rosalind liked the old words, said they tasted nicer in the mouth. She got poetic sometimes, especially when the dusk turned the air to honey. (Is it even possible for air to do that? I dunno, but she was convincing.)

On one of those slow afternoons, while the bees made drowsy music, Jaques said, “Do you ever wonder why we’re all here, together?” Rosalind threw a pebble at him—gently—and said, “Obviously, for the company.” I just shrugged, because what else can you say? Maybe it’s true. Maybe we all just find our people by accident and hang on till the next season pulls us somewhere else.

Honestly, sometimes I think the talk mattered more than the answers. Like, we’d circle around the same questions—about love or luck or whether squirrels ever feel lonely—never really settling anything. But there was something kind of perfect about not knowing, about just letting the words tumble out and hang between us.

He tore the page out, folded it small, and slipped it in her palm when she wasn’t looking. Later, I saw her open it—just for a second—and smile at the sky like she’d won some secret game.

So that’s how it was, I guess. A bunch of us, filling the air with questions and half-serious answers, pretending not to care and caring a whole lot all the same. Maybe nothing happened, or maybe everything did—I’m still not sure. But sometimes I close my eyes and I can almost hear Rosalind

So, look, I’m gonna tell you how it went down, like, the way it really happened. Don’t expect a fairytale or whatever, because that’s just not… I mean, come on, have you ever met anyone as loud as Falstaff? He barges into the little upstairs room at the Garter, smells like rain and cheap ale, and just shouts for the Host like he owns the joint. The thing is, everyone lets him. Why? I dunno. Maybe he’s got that kinda energy. Sir Page is already there, half asleep on a bench, and honestly, I don't blame him. Would you want to listen to another one of Falstaff’s schemes?

But then Pistol comes clinking in, all metal and noise, waving his hat and talking about honor—like he even remembers what it is. Sir, I swear, if you could put a price on empty words, Pistol’d be the richest man in Windsor. And Nym’s not far behind, sort of lurking at the doorway, mumbling about how things'll end up bad. Nym always expects the worst. Probably right half the time, must be exhausting.

Slender comes last. He’s got that spindly look, like a stick with a fancy coat, and he keeps glancing at the windows like he's expecting someone to throw a shoe at his head again. That kind of thing happens to him, you know? He just draws trouble. Anyway, everyone’s in place, sorta, and the Host’s fussing with mugs at the bar, not even pretending to pay them any mind.

So there they are, making this weird little circle. Falstaff's got his feet up, Pistol's bragging about some duel or something, and Slender keeps whispering to Page, probably because he's too scared to ask for a drink himself. Do you ever wonder how people like this become friends? Or maybe they're not even friends. Maybe they're just stuck together because nobody else can stand them. I dunno. Makes you think.

There's this bit, where Falstaff tries to convince them about a plan—something involving a rich widow, some disguises, and, uh, a goose. Don’t ask me, I couldn't follow it, and neither could Page, from the look on his face. Pistol yells about "fortune favoring the bold" and nearly knocks over a chair, and Nym mutters, "words, words, words," like he's some kind of philosopher. Slender just nods, not understanding a word, but wanting to seem in the know.

And the Host? He finally walks over, wiping his hands on his apron, and just says, "If you break anything, you're paying." That's all. No patience for drama, no time for fools. Pretty much sums up the whole place.

But here's the funny part—despite all their nonsense, there's this little moment when they're all laughing. I mean, Falstaff's joke is terrible (it has something to do with a parrot and a church bell), but everyone laughs anyway. For a second, they're not scheming or worrying or pretending to be braver than they are. They're just… I dunno, happy? Maybe. It passes quick, but it's real.

Then, as you'd expect, some actual trouble walks through the door. Two big men in smart coats, nobody recognizes them, and everyone just freezes. Falstaff tries to act like he's the king, Pistol's hand slips to the knife at his belt, and Nym's already heading for the back. Slender tries to hide behind Page, but Page is too tired to move. The Host rolls his eyes so hard you could hear it.

Turns out, the men are just lost. Ask for directions, take one awkward look at the group, and leave almost as fast as they came in. The whole room exhales, and Falstaff says, "You see, men, destiny awaits the bold." Like, sure, that's what just happened. Everybody knows it isn't, but nobody says otherwise. And anyway, that's kinda how it goes, right?

So there it ends for the night. The Host closes up, Falstaff promises to pay next week, Pistol and Nym bicker all the way out the door, and Slender forgets his hat. Page grabs it for him. They spill into the street, still arguing about something pointless, but smiling. You ever watch people who seem wrong together but, somehow, they make it work? That's them. And honestly, I wouldn't change a thing about it.

So, I guess the thing is, Syracuse isn’t what people think. It’s more like the name you give to that feeling of missing your bus by exactly two seconds, or dropping your keys and hearing them bounce just out of reach. It’s Syracuse, it’s time, it’s never quite being where you’re supposed to be. Have you ever felt that? Probably. I mean, who hasn’t?

So, yeah, sometimes you’ll hear people calling out from windows or alleys, and you’ll think, “Was that for me?” It’s almost never for you, but, like, what if it was? And honestly, most days you don’t even bother with it. You just keep walking, maybe tug your jacket closer, and watch the shadows get longer. The thing is, Syracuse isn’t cold, exactly, but there’s this weird chill that always sneaks up around your ankles, like it’s trying to remind you of something you forgot to do. Y’know, every city’s got its own way of saying, “Don’t get comfortable.”

There’s this clock tower near the center, and it’s always running three minutes fast. Someone said that’s on purpose, but honestly, I think nobody knows how to fix it. I mean, who would bother? Time isn’t really linear here. It’s more like a circle, or maybe a spiral. When you’re waiting for a friend—let’s call him Antipholus because why not—you’ll check your phone, look up at the clock, and realize it’s never the time you expect. Sometimes, you’ll stand there so long, you forget what day it is.

So, when night falls—by the way, night comes quick here, like you blink and all the streetlights are on—you might wonder where the time went. Have you ever sat on a bench and watched the way the lights flicker and wondered, “Why am I still here?” The answer, I guess, is you’re waiting for something. Maybe it’s Antipholus, maybe it’s Dromio, maybe it’s just the next bus, who knows. People in Syracuse aren’t in a hurry, but they’re never really just standing still either. It’s all about moving, even if you’re not sure where.

Oh, and one more thing—there’s a sort of hush after midnight, like the city’s holding its breath. If you’re brave, or maybe just curious, you can walk the quiet streets and listen. Sometimes, you’ll hear footsteps behind you, but when you turn, there's nobody. Other times, you’ll swear you hear your name called, soft and far away. It makes you wonder, is it the city calling for you? Or is it just your imagination, messing with you the way Syracuse always does?

There's a kind of comfort in that, even if you've got no idea where you're going, or why. All you’ve got is the city, the time, and whoever happens to call your name. After a while, she came to a little bridge. It was rickety, kind of crooked, but she thought, “I’ll cross it, why not?” There was no one around, nobody to ask her if she was sure, and that actually made her feel brave—maybe too brave, because she ran across the bridge and almost slipped, catching herself at the last second. “Okay, maybe I’m not that brave,” she muttered, but laughed a little, too. The air on the other side felt colder, though, and she shivered. Could’ve gone back, but she felt like that’d be cheating, so she pressed on.

You know, she remembered something her grandmother used to say, about how there were places where the world felt thinner, where you could almost hear the other side whispering. Elizabeth thought, “If anyone could find something strange, it’d be me,” and that was enough to keep her going, even though her shoes pinched and she was pretty sure she’d lost a sock somewhere. And honestly, it’s crazy how much we forget about day-to-day stuff, like how hungry you are, until you’re out there, alone. Elizabeth wasn’t sure if she could make it, but she didn’t want to give up just yet.

She found a bench—just one, out in the middle of nowhere, and sat down. The thing is, she could’ve stayed there forever, or at least until someone came by and told her to move, but nobody did. There was a squirrel, though, and she tried to talk to it, because why not? “Hey, little guy, do you think I’m going to find what I’m looking for?” The squirrel didn’t answer, obviously (wouldn’t that be something?), but she felt a little better. Sometimes you just need to say things out loud, even if it’s to a squirrel.

She thought about her family, and wondered if they’d be worried, or maybe just annoyed. Could anybody actually miss her that much? And then she thought about her old friends, the ones who’d moved away or drifted, and she realized she couldn’t remember the last time she’d been really happy. Maybe happiness isn’t something you find, she thought, maybe it’s something you make. But truthfully, she wasn’t sure, and didn’t believe in easy answers.

It started to rain, and Elizabeth pulled her jacket tighter, but stayed on that bench. Some part of her figured the rain would make her feel cleansed or renewed, but really it just made her socks soggy. She could go back, but what would she say? “I left because I was looking for something, and I found a bench and a squirrel and some rain.” Not much of a story, right? But maybe that’s how it goes.

Eventually, as the day faded, she stood up and started walking again, not really expecting much, but not giving up either. She believed, or at least wanted to believe, that something good could happen, even if she didn’t know what it was. And honestly, isn’t that what keeps people going? She thought so.

So, you wanna hear about the old Water Street project? I mean, it’s not exactly a story for the ages, but hey, why not. The thing is, when I first got assigned to that block, I figured it’d be more of the same—just a bunch of guys in reflective vests, some busted pipes, a few half-hearted arguments with local shop owners. Honestly, I’d seen it all before, or so I thought. But I guess every project’s got its own weird flavor.

I remember the first morning, walking up to the site with my hands jammed in my pockets. It was colder than I’d expected, and Oscar was already cursing at the backhoe, waving his arms around like he was in some kind of opera. You ever notice how some workmen can make a scene out of nothing? Oscar’s a master at that.

We’d been told to expect “complications,” which is just supervisor-speak for “we have no idea what’s under this street and you’re gonna hate it.” And, I mean, they were right. The facts were all over the place—old maps didn’t match, and nobody could agree where the sewer line actually ran. I tried to look like I knew what I was doing, but, you know, you can only fake it so much when mud’s up past your ankles.

The workmen started tearing up the pavement around noon, and let me tell you, the sound was unreal. Not just the machines—though that grinding got into your teeth—but the way the whole neighborhood seemed to come out of nowhere. Some guy with a purple dog kept asking if we’d seen his missing mailbox. A bakery owner brought out coffee, like, four hours late. There’s just something about construction that draws people in, even if all they’re gonna get is noise and blocked driveways.

We put in the steel plates, started digging, and, I swear, every foot down was a new surprise. Oscar found some old bottle, all green and crusty, and started theorizing about pirates. I’m not saying it was impossible, but come on. The guy thinks everything’s a treasure. But then, who’s to say what’s valuable? I guess, after a while, weird bits of stuff are all you’ve got.

By the third day, morale was shot. Rain had filled the pit, and the backhoe had eaten someone’s lunch by mistake. Don’t even ask. I remember thinking—why do we put up with this? Is it the paycheck, or just the stubbornness to see something finished? Some days, it’s hard to tell. The crew was soaked, and the only thing holding everyone together was Frank’s terrible jokes. You try laughing at a guy who tells the same line every morning for a week straight.

Now, the facts, as far as they go, were pretty clear: something was blocking the main line, and nobody wanted to admit it could be a collapsed wall. The city rep insisted it must be a tree root, but we all knew better. You could feel it in the way the shovels hit—there was a kind of hollow thud that made no sense. Would you trust a city map made in 1956? ‘Cause I certainly wouldn’t.

We argued and cursed, but in the end, we did what we always do. Oscar crawled in with the flashlight, found a brick arch that shouldn’t have been there, swore a blue streak, and then we called it in. Some engineer showed up with a stack of forms and an attitude that could’ve cut steel. “Just patch it and move on,” he said, barely looking down.

I guess, the thing is, you start out thinking you’ll make a big difference, fix something important—but most days, you just do your bit and try not to ruin anything. By the time we filled the trench and cleaned up the trash, nobody cared about the old archway. We certainly didn’t. Well, maybe Oscar did. Sometimes I still wonder, did it really matter what we found down there, or was it just work, like always?

Anyway, next week there’s another street and more mud. Maybe this time the only thing we’ll dig up is dirt. But I wouldn’t bet on it.

If you’ve ever seen someone who’s so used to their own disappointment that it just sits on their shoulders like a jacket, but a tight one, you know what I mean. Anna didn’t get it, though. I could see in the way she clenched her fists, holding back a question she’d already asked too many times. Did he ever wish things were different? Or was that just what she wanted him to admit, so she could let herself off the hook?

And honestly, that’s the thing that stuck with me: the stuff we wish people would call theirs. Some people think that’s rude, but Linton wasn’t about politeness—not in that way. He was careful, though. He’d wait for you to accept or not, and if you didn’t, well, the moment was gone.
