So, like, you probably haven’t met Oliver, right? Or maybe you have and just didn’t realize, because he’s got this sort of background-person vibe, but also—well, okay, he stands out if you look for it. His brother, Charles, is the type you’d notice more, but we’ll get to him in a sec. Right now, let’s just say Oliver’s always got mud on his boots. Even when it isn’t raining. Figure that one out.

The funny thing is, they grew up in the same house, with their father, who wasn’t, uh, really fatherly, if you get what I mean. But he was a duke. Which means, supposedly, he’s all dignified and noble, and whatever else dukes are meant to be. But all people talked about was how he loved his old hunting dogs more than his sons. Maybe it was true? Wouldn’t be the weirdest thing.

Now, Orlando enters the picture. He’s Charles’s friend—or sometimes you’d think rival, since they’re like two goats butting heads over everything. Orlando’s got ideas. Big ones. Sometimes too big for the town they live in. He’d roll up to the edge of the estate, stare out at the foggy fields, then say stuff like, “This land’s all bones, I swear.” Which, what does that even mean? But people listened, because Orlando’s got a voice that makes you wanna hear what he says, even if it’s nonsense. Or is it?

Meanwhile, Sir John—that’s another character who just pops up whenever there’s food or trouble (those two go hand in hand for him). Sir John isn’t actually a knight, but insists on the ‘Sir.’ Nobody really argues, because, you know, why pick a fight with a guy who knows where every secret wine cellar is?

So back to the brothers. One rainy night, Charles is pacing outside, muttering about inheritance. You’d think he’d be excited, but nah, he’s wringing his hands and looking like a ghost. Oliver finds him there, huddled under a dying sycamore. “You out here planning a revolution, or just freezing?” Oliver asks, but Charles shakes his head.

The thing is, Charles never really wanted the lands, or the house, or the headaches that come with it. What he wanted—well, he couldn’t say, but it sure wasn’t what was waiting inside that old stone house. Sometimes I wonder, did any of them really want this life, or were they just sort of handed it like a soggy package and told, “Here’s your future, don’t drop it”? Who decides that, huh?

Then the father, the duke, shuffles past with his cane and two dogs trailing, like a parade of the past. He doesn’t say much anymore. If he did, it’d probably just be about the dogs’ latest adventure in the duck pond. There’s a distance between him and his sons like a whole ocean, and no one’s got a boat.

Honestly, I think Oliver always wanted to leave. He’d watch birds a lot, the kind that fly in crooked flocks, not the pretty ones people put on greeting cards. He’d say, “That’s freedom, right there,” but not loud enough for anyone but himself to hear. Why stick around, then? Is it hope, or just habit?

Anyway, one morning, after the mist burned off and left the fields looking almost beautiful, Orlando bursts in with a wild idea about digging up some old well, convinced there’s something amazing hidden down there. Sir John’s already got his sleeves rolled up, thinking there’ll be a bottle if he helps. It turns into this half-baked adventure, mud everywhere, Charles pretending he doesn’t care, but of course he does—he’s got dirt on his shoes to prove it.

They don’t find treasure, unless you count a rusty horseshoe and a pile of broken crockery treasure. Orlando laughs so hard he falls backwards, and for a second, everyone’s just people, not sons or dukes or anything that heavy. Just four muddy guys, making a mess.

Later, when the sun’s nearly gone and the dogs have given up begging for scraps, Charles sits with Oliver by the kitchen door. The cook forgot to shut it and you can smell bread in the air. For once, there’s nothing left to argue about. Maybe tomorrow, something’ll change, or maybe they’ll just keep walking these same old fields, but together, and that isn’t so bad.

Anyway, that’s the story, or at least, that’s how it feels when you’re there. Does any of this matter in the end? Maybe not. But then, maybe it’s just about being seen, even if it’s only by a brother with mud on his boots.

All right, okay—so you want me to tell it like I remember it, yeah? Not the cleaned-up version, just, you know, as it happened, tangled up bits and all. I’m not gonna make it pretty. So. There we were, in the brambles near the old stone wall, somewhere past dusk but not quite real dark, and honestly, I was thinking more about whether the rain would hold off than, like, the fate of the world or anything. You ever stand out there and just, uh, wonder what absolutely possessed you to come along? That was me. Anyway, Cade kept whispering, “Come away, thou fool, move,” as if the bushes could hear him. And you can’t be mad at Cade for being like that, ‘cause he’s always been jumpy, but I was about ready to leave him there.

But the thing is, we’d heard there was a lord’s men coming through, yeah, a whole mess of ‘em, and word got around that Lord Farn kept a chest of silver on the road. And—before you get sanctimonious or whatever—no, we weren’t planning on robbing them exactly, just…watching. Seeing if maybe fortune would smile on us, or if not, at least we’d have something good to talk about later. Cade though, he had stars in his eyes about it, speaking low like, “What say you, shall we take our chance?” and I’m just thinking, have you ever seen us win a fight? Or run quick enough? But, you know, he was my mate.

So there we waited, crouched ‘til my knees cracked, while Cade muttered oaths he must’ve heard in church. That’s the funny part… We’re supposed to be grown men but if you’d seen us, you’d have thought we were two feral cats if anything. There was a shuffling, the soft clank of armour, and, well, my stomach dropped clean out of me. I reckon I wasn’t the only one holding their breath.

Next thing, the lord’s men come in a little cluster, not looking around much. These weren’t polished knights—just men, tired, grumbling, with beards and muddy boots and less silver than Cade was hoping for. I almost felt bad for ‘em. Almost. One said, “Hast thou any bread left?” and the other just grunted, so I guess we weren’t the only ones hungry. Isn’t that funny, how you think lords’ men would eat better than us? Ha.

Cade grabbed my sleeve, hard, and whispered, “Now, come away, afore they see us.” Something in his voice, I dunno, made my legs move on their own. We stumbled back through the brambles, making so much noise a blind owl coulda tracked us, but the men didn’t turn. They just kept walking, bent under cold and rain, and I thought, what’s the use of lords and loyalty if you’re just wet and hungry all the time? Like, seriously, who are they to us?

We got far enough to breathe easy, and Cade—he, uh, started laughing, really laughing, not the fake kind he does when he’s scared. It was almost a relief. I found myself laughing too, and suddenly it all seemed pointless and sort of wonderful, like we’d seen some secret no one else knew. I mean, what did we actually have, except our own two feet and a friend who’d drag you out of trouble instead of into it? Maybe that’s enough.

So no, we didn’t become outlaws or find a chest of silver. We just went home muddy, hungry, and a little less worried about the world. ‘Cause, you know, at the end of it all, you’ve got to ask, what’s left when you take away the lords and the men and all their noise? Just us, walking home, laughing about nothing. Maybe that’s all anyone really needs.

The friar kind of patted his shoulder, like, “Thou must be strong,” but you could see this look, maybe thinking, “Kid, you have no idea.”

You might wonder: did the friar actually believe he was helping? I guess so. He mixed up some powders and wrote a letter. That’s where John comes in—Friar John, not just any John, you know? He was supposed to take the message and, I dunno, make things better. But he got stuck somewhere, plague or locked doors, something like that. Meanwhile, Romeo’s pacing, probably saying, “What news, good friar? Is she safe?” And the friar was sweating bullets, probably. Okay, hang on, let me see if I can tell this story the way it actually happened, or at least the way I remember it, because, you know, memory’s weird. So. I’m standing there in the kitchen, and Lennox is pacing like he’s about to wear a hole through the linoleum, and there’s this smell, onions or maybe something burning, but I don’t care, not with the storm coming. The wind’s already howling around the gutters, and the branches keep scraping the windows like bony old fingers. I tell Lennox to sit down and he just says, “No, I can’t, I really can’t,” and kind of waves his hand in that way he does when he’s freaked out.

The thing is, none of this would’ve happened if it weren’t for that damn letter from the lord. You ever get, like, one of those pieces of mail that just feels... heavier? As if the envelope’s hiding something alive inside it? Well, this one did, and I didn’t wanna open it, but Lennox practically snatched it outta my hands.

So, yeah, he tears it open and there’s this summons, all formal and fancy, with a stamp and the lord’s creepy seal. “They want me to come,” he says, but really what I hear is “We’re in trouble.” Because who gets called to the old manor on a night like this and comes back the same?

And honestly, you have to know Lennox. He’s not brave. I mean, he tries, but his hands shake, especially around authority. This whole “go see the lord” thing, it’s eating him alive. He sits, finally, and starts tapping the table like he’s playing some code.

Then—you’re not gonna believe me, but whatever—the air goes cold. You know when a room just drops, like maybe you left the freezer door wide open? And outta nowhere there’s this... smell? Not the onions, not the burning—something sharp and earthy, like rain on stones, or, okay, like grave dirt. My skin goes prickly and suddenly there’s this woman in the corner, right by the broken lamp. I swear she wasn’t there before.

She’s just standing there, and I can’t make out her face, not fully. Her voice is kind of everywhere at once, but somehow soft. “You shall not go,” she says, and I wanna scream, but my mouth won’t work. Lennox is staring—he’s got that look, wide-eyed, like he’s seeing a car crash in slow motion and can’t decide whether to look away or keep watching.

But, um, here’s the thing: we’ve both heard stories about the witch by the willows. Kids always dared each other to see if she’d show up, never thinking she actually would. And yet, there she is, in my kitchen, acting like she owns the place. Her skirt’s trailing mud on my tile and I actually think, stupidly, about how I’ll clean it later.

She turns to me, and, well, I’m not gonna pretend I’m brave either. “Lord Lennox can’t answer that call,” she says—wait, I never called him Lord Lennox, that’s just weird—and I realize she’s staring at me like I’m supposed to argue, but I just... can’t. I don’t even know if she’s talking to me or to something in the walls.

So, uh, yeah, Lennox finally manages to squeak out, “Why not? What’ll happen if I do?” And she just smiles, all teeth, and says, “You come, and you won’t come back. The lord needs someone, but it won’t be you—not if I can help it.”

There’s this silence after she speaks, not awkward but thick, if that makes sense. Rain starts hitting the window harder and the lights flicker, like every ghost in town’s shaking the lines. Lennox and I just look at each other, both thinking about the stories and whether they’re warnings or just old nonsense you tell kids to keep them in at night.

But, like, what do you do when the witch actually comes to you? What do you say when you’re told not to answer the call? Lennox starts to say something else, but she’s gone, like she never existed, and the smell fades just as quick. The only thing left is a muddy footprint where she stood and the letter, still on the table, like a dare.

I wish I could say we were brave, that we faced it, but honestly we just sat there, listening to the storm and waiting for morning. I still don’t know if I did the right thing. Do you?

I shouted for my sword (which, honestly, was more for show than anything), and everyone around me scrambled with big, frightened eyes. So, you know how it is out on the water, when you’re the first one to set foot on the sand after a long night tossing in the boat? The air’s heavy with salt, and even though it’s supposed to be spring, somehow the wind finds its way right under your coat. Anyway, there was this guy—old Pericles, they called him, but only when he wasn’t around. He would come down to the shore around dawn, every day, looking all thoughtful like he expected some secret to pop right out of the waves. Honestly, I never knew what he was hoping to find. Maybe a message in a bottle or, I don’t know, a sign from the gods or something.

And then there’s Simonides. That’s me, by the way, though pretty much everyone just calls me 'Simon.' I’d like to say I was the village’s best fisherman, but that’d be a stretch—maybe top three if I’m lucky, and only because old Rhys hasn’t caught anything worth talking about in years. Still, I’ve been out before sunrise since I was a kid, so I suppose I know the ropes. Some days, I’ll tell you, fish’ll jump right into your nets, and some other days you’d swear they’ve all packed up and left the sea.

So this morning, well, I was untangling my line, half-listening for the gulls, when Pericles comes pacing up. You ever seen a man so lost in his head he trips over his own feet? That was him that day. He stops, stares at the water, then sort of sighs and glances at me.

“Simonides,” he says, and he always uses my full name, “you ever think about what’s out there?” He points past the rocks, toward the open blue where the sun is just starting to break up the mist.

Well, what do you say to that? I shrugged, said, “Fish, I hope.” 

He laughs, but it’s a tired sort of laugh, you know? The kind people use when they’ve got bigger worries than fish. “No,” he says, “I mean, really—do you ever feel as though something’s calling you from out there?”

Now, I’d like to say I’m the kind of fellow who’s got answers for everything. But I guess I sort of shifted my feet and mumbled something about the only thing that ever called me was an empty stomach.

Pericles just keeps on staring. “I had a dream of Thaisa,” he says. His voice gets real quiet, and I almost pretend not to hear. “She was standing on the shore, just—just over there, by the old willow. She called to me. And it was her, I know it was.” 

The thing is, most folks don’t talk too much about Thaisa anymore. She was his wife, or maybe more like a legend by now—disappeared in a storm, years back. Some say she drowned, some say she ran off to another village, but you know how stories grow around here. All I know is, Pericles never quite got over it.

So, I didn’t want to poke at old wounds. But I had to say something, right? “You figure dreams mean something, sir?” I asked, trying to keep my voice steady.

He smiled, that sad way he does. “Sometimes. Sometimes I think it’s just the sea, whispering in my sleep. Other times, I think… maybe I’m meant to go after her.”

Now, tell me, what would you do if a man like Pericles turned to you and said he might be pulled out to sea by a voice only he could hear? There’s not much you can do, really. I tried to joke. “Well then, you’ll need a bigger net, sir.”

He actually chuckled, a real one this time, and patted my shoulder. But I could see it in his eyes—he’d already set sail in his head, whether his boat left shore or not.

So, we fished. Caught two mackerel, nothing special. The sun came up, burned off the grey. Pericles wandered off by noon, same as always, and I packed up my catch and started up the path. I always pass that old willow on my way home. Call me superstitious, but sometimes the hairs on my neck stand up there, like someone’s watching. Is it just the wind, or do old stories hang around longer than we think?

Anyway, that’s how it goes. The fish come in, the fish go out. The sea keeps her secrets, and men like Pericles keep listening. And me? I just mend my nets and wait for tomorrow, same as always.

You get this weird feeling that the castle itself is listening. And maybe, just maybe, it remembers more than all of them put together.

So uh, this is a pretty weird story, but you wanted one, so here goes. There was this guy, his name was—well, I’m not gonna say his name straight out because, you know, names have power or whatever, but let’s call him “R.” So, R was, you know, kind of a mess in the way that people get when they’re young and think they know how it all works, but I don’t think he really did. He’d wander around at night, just talking to himself, or maybe not talking, more like muttering. 

The thing is, he had this huge thing for a girl. And, ugh, can you believe it? Her folks hated his, like, ancient, grudge-style hatred where nobody can even remember why they’re mad. So, anyway, this guy—R—he would hang out under her window and sometimes throw rocks but, you know, carefully, because he didn’t wanna break anything. He’d say stuff like, “If only my name wasn’t mine,” and then get all quiet like he’d said something important. What’s a name, really, you know? Sometimes you start wondering if you’re just all the labels people stick on you or if you can be more than that.

I mean, how much do names matter? Like, if I woke up tomorrow and everyone called me “Zebra,” would I start acting stripy and wild? Or would I just stay myself and get used to being shouted at in a new way? That’s the kind of dumb question “R” would actually ask. And if you called him out—like, “Hey, you’re being dramatic”—he’d just sigh and look at the moon like it owed him money.

But, sorry, back on track. One night, the girl—let’s call her “J”—shows up at her window and she’s got this serious look, like she’s been waiting her whole life to say something. R nearly falls over seeing her, and starts in with, “What’s in a name?” and all that. He thinks if he could just drop his name, everything would be fine. Like, presto, all the problems vanish. But would they? If he was still who he was inside, would anything really change, or would the world just find something else to gripe about?

J shakes her head—she’s got this way of listening, but not letting him get away with stuff. She says, “Would you toss away everything for me?” and R tries to make some big speech, but he can’t get the words out in the right order. Have you ever tried to say something important and just ended up babbling? Happens all the time to me. Words get stuck. It's like the more you care, the harder it gets.

So anyway, the two of them go back and forth, and, honestly, it’s about as awkward as you’d expect. Love can be, what, clumsy? It’s not all perfect lines and swooning. Sometimes it’s just two people tripping over how much they wish things were easier. Like, wouldn’t it be nice if the world just chilled out and let people love who they wanted to, no drama? Ha—good one, right?

But here’s the weird part. R tries to make a promise—he starts with, “By thy name, I swear,” or something, then he stops and laughs. He says, “Wait, what am I even swearing by? The thing I said I’d give up?” and they both just crack up. The moon looks on, and, well, I dunno if the moon cared, but it was there.

You ever notice moments like that sort of float? Like, maybe they don’t solve anything, but for a second, you feel lighter, like the world’s nonsense doesn’t stick quite so hard. The two of them—R and J—they decide, right there, that love isn’t about the name or the old stories or anybody else’s rules. It’s about… well, nobody really knows, do they? That’s it, really. No fancy ending. Just people hoping the world lets them be themselves for once. Do you suppose that ever happens?

So, here's the thing—I mean, if you had asked old Fluellen, he'd've sworn up and down that the king knew everything. Like, not just the big stuff either, but every single pebble in the courtyard, every little gust of wind, who ate what for breakfast—I mean, you get the idea, right? But, honestly, if you pressed him, Fluellen had never actually seen the king doing any of those things. He just sort of, well, believed it. Maybe it's easier that way when you're following someone into battle or, I dunno, handing out punishments for rotten apples. You gotta trust. Or pretend to trust.

Now, Henry—yeah, King Henry—the lad didn't really look like he knew much. Not at first glance, you know? He had this way of blinking, kind of slow, like the world had just flicked his ear, and he was deciding if it was worth getting up about it. But, the thing is, people started talking about him the minute he left a room. Like, "Did you hear what he said to Montjoy?" or "What do you think he meant about the pridge?" (Yeah, "pridge," not "bridge." Don't ask me why. It was always "pridge" with Fluellen and his lot.)

Anyway, Montjoy—he's the messenger, if you're keeping track—he knew something was cooking. You could see it in the way he fidgeted with his hat, squashing the brim down until it looked like a pie crust. I mean, who wears a hat like that? So, he stands there, right in front of Henry, all bowing and scraping, and you know he's wishing he was anywhere else in the world. Maybe back in France, or at least out of sight.

"Is it well with you, Montjoy?" Henry asks, and it sounds like nothing special, but—this is the thing—everyone leans forward, like he's about to drop the answer to life itself. And Montjoy, he just blinks and says, "Well enough, sire." There's about four heartbeats of silence, and Fluellen snorts, like he's choking on something, and someone else coughs for no reason.

And then, I kid you not, Henry just grins. Like, not a king's grin. A real grin, crooked and unsure and, maybe, a little tired. Says, "Well, that's good, 'cause I was worried for a moment you might've lost your way." And—oh man—the look on Montjoy's face! Like, what do you even say to that? Did the king just joke with him, threaten him, or what? I don't know. Nobody did.

But here's the bit that got me, and, yeah, you can call me a sentimental fool, but it's true: later, when everyone had wandered off, Henry sat down by himself, on this old bench under the willows. He just sat there. Hands in his lap, humming some old song, kind of off-key. I watched him, I admit it—yeah, maybe I should've left, but sometimes you just want to know what a king does when nobody's looking, you know? He looked...well, not lonely, but like he'd forgotten something important, and wasn't sure he could remember.

I guess that's what being king is. Everyone walks around thinking you know everything, and really, half the time you don't even know what's in your own head. Or, you pretend not to. Maybe it's better that way. Wouldn't you do the same if you had to wear that heavy crown and wave to people and act like you weren't scared, even once in a while?

Fluellen used to say, "The pridge is the thing, mark you," but I think maybe he was just talking to fill the air. You know how people do. Sometimes, the words we say don't matter as much as the silences after. And honestly, that's the part I remember. Not Henry's speeches, or the messengers with their grand bows, but the quiet, when the king hummed and nobody else was near.

So, I dunno, maybe kings don't need to know everything. Maybe they're just like the rest of us, bluffing through, hoping nobody notices the cracks. And if that's true—well, isn't that kind of a relief?

So, the thing is, Timon’s house used to be the one with the golden roof — not really gold, of course, but you’d look at it and for a second, you’d buy it. He threw open those double doors every night like he wanted to let in the whole city. Lords, poets, hangers-on, folks looking for a free drink — they all crowded in, laughing too loud, talking too fast. There was a story going round that some guy, a merchant or a painter or, I don’t know, a juggler, once walked in not even knowing Timon, and left with a horse and a bag of coins.

But now? You’d walk up his drive and see weeds taller than your head, windows all dusty, that golden color faded to something that looks like, I don’t know, like rain on pavement. The only person coming and going anymore is Flavius. He’s Timon’s steward — loyal to a fault. You get the sense he’s the last one holding the place together, but for what? Who’s he keeping the house for? Timon barely eats, sits with his back to the fire most nights, muttering to himself. And if you ask where the lords went, or all those bright-eyed friends — well, aren’t you just asking for disappointment?

I saw Apemantus out there once too. He’s something else, that guy. You never know if he’s making fun of you or just stating facts, but he’s always scowling like someone put vinegar in his wine. He stood in Timon’s hall, looked around, and just said, “Well, you’ve emptied your purse, and emptied your house right after. Who’s the fool?” But Timon just shrugged. He didn’t even argue. He mostly doesn’t bother anymore. Is it just me, or do people get tired even of being angry? Maybe there’s only so much cursing one person can manage before it all feels pointless.

Sometimes, when Timon’s not in his own head, he’ll ask Flavius about old friends. “What about Lord Lucius?” he’ll say. “He owed me a favor.” And Flavius, poor soul, he’ll say he sent messages, but nobody answered. Doesn’t that sting? Giving everything you’ve got to folks who vanish at the first sign you might need something back. Do you think people are selfish by nature, or is it just easy to forget the hand that fed you once you’re full?

Timon used to bless everyone who visited — I mean, really, like toast to their good health, wish them luck, all that. Now he looks tired even when he tries to smile. And sometimes he says stuff that doesn’t even make sense, like, “The sun’s nothing but a lamp burning out.” I don’t know what that means, honestly. Maybe it’s how it gets when you’ve seen so much hope slip away.

But Flavius keeps going. He sweeps, he lights candles, he fixes the drapes no one’s looking at. He still calls Timon “my lord”, even when there’s no one left to hear. That kind of loyalty, it’s either heartwarming or just sad. Depends how you see it.

I’ll tell you, one night I stayed late in the kitchen, just passing time with the old cook, and we heard Timon stomping around in the dark, cursing the walls, like the house itself had betrayed him, not the people. The cook just shook his head, said, “When the gold’s gone, so’s the laughter.” That stuck with me.

So, days pass, nights drag on, and the city forgets Timon. He could’ve been remembered as a generous soul, I guess, but who writes down the stories of men who give everything away? One morning, I saw Flavius standing out front, waiting for a letter or a knock that didn’t come, and I thought, well, maybe that’s the real fool’s errand — hoping people remember, or care, or come back.

And honestly, I can’t decide if Timon’s the idiot for loving people so much, or if everyone else is for forgetting him the second the silver ran dry. Maybe that’s just how it goes, though. Not sure. All I know is, the house is quiet now. Too quiet. Sometimes, you almost think you can hear laughter echoing off the empty walls, but it’s just the wind. Or maybe ghosts, who knows.

So, uncle sits us down—me and Phoebe—and says, “There’s a spirit in the study.” The way he says it, like he’s telling us we’re out of milk, not that there’s, you know, an actual ghost hanging out with the chessboard. Uncle explains that someone—he whispers “Hume,” which is just wild, because Hume’s been dead for at least a hundred years—has been knocking things off shelves, and sometimes you just hear sighing, not like the house sighing, but a person. He swears he saw, quote, “a flicker and the shaking of Lord Bolingbroke’s old walking stick.” Phoebe asks, “Does the ghost have a schedule, or is it freelance haunting?” I didn’t laugh, but it was a good question.

So, let’s just—well, look, I’ll start from where I remember. It was Martius, yeah, always kind of, I don’t know, he just had that blunt way about him, right? Not exactly the guy you’d take to a festival if you wanted to have fun, but for getting stuff done, you’d want him right there. And so it happened, or maybe it nearly did (memory’s weird), but he and Cominius were standing out by that ugly old wall near the gate, watching soldiers shuffle around. Lartius was supposed to meet them, but, you know, he’s late. Typical.

The thing is, Martius couldn’t sit still at all. He kept clapping mud off his gloves, pacing back and forth, and it’s like—honestly, why do people like him get stuck waiting around so much? He’s built for action. So he starts in, “Cominius, we could be halfway to Aufidius’ camp by now, if folks would just pull together instead of talking everything apart.” And Cominius just shrugs, but you can tell he’s tired of all the noise too.

Maybe you’re wondering what any of this has to do with anything, but, well, I guess it’s the way they all acted that kind of sticks with me. It was like nobody could agree on what was actually ‘good’ for us, or the city, or whatever. Everyone had a different story. Martius thought it was simple—you’re either on the side that fixes what’s wrong, or you’re the thing that’s wrong. Hard lines, no gray zone. But Cominius, and Lartius too when he finally got there, kept trying to talk things through. “Let’s not rush, let’s hear both sides, let’s be careful.” That sort of thing. Does being careful ever make a difference when things are falling apart, though?

And all the while, little rumors about Aufidius are floating around, like dark water under a bridge. That he’s gathering more folks, or he’s got spies—can’t ever pin it down, but it gets people nervous. Martius kind of fed off that, almost got sharper with every new bit of bad news. Sometimes, I thought maybe he actually wanted the fight just to cut through all the noise. There was this weird moment, I remember it pretty clear, where Martius just turns and asks—half to himself, half to us—“If we know what needs doing, what’s the point in waiting for someone else to say so?” And, well, you know, no one said anything for a bit.

Lartius, he’s always the practical one, starts talking about moving supplies, getting the gates checked. You’d think they’d be working together by then, but you could feel something pulling apart underneath, like, I don’t know, a rope fraying where nobody’s looking.

Later that day, after the dust and the yelling, I saw Martius by himself over by the wall. He looked angry, but not the good kind. Not the kind that makes you want to, you know, do something bold. It was heavy and cold. Like he was carrying a rock nobody else could see. People kept saying he’d done good. But good’s a slippery word, isn’t it? What does it even mean, when everyone sees it different? 

Honestly, I’m not sure what happened with Aufidius in the end. The stories got tangled, and there’s always another war or peace or argument coming right after. But—uh—I’ll tell you, sometimes, when you’re out by the wall, you can almost feel old Martius’ footsteps still there. People talk about honor and duty and all that, but they never tell you how it’s supposed to feel after you’ve done what needed doing. Would you want to know?

In any case, I guess some things keep going. Even when people change, or names get lost, there’s always someone standing at a wall, deciding if they should wait or go. And, uh, maybe that’s the real question. If you knew what needed doing, would you just get on with it, or would you wait for someone else to tell you it’s alright?

It was just about evening, and well, honestly, I wasn’t even sure why I’d come out to the old house again. It’s cold, you know, with that wind that whips through your jacket and makes your teeth knock together. Heathcliff was already sitting on the porch when I got there, legs stretched out like he owned the whole place. I mean, maybe he did, but it’s not like anybody else wanted it. He looked at me sideways and, instead of saying hello, he just sort of grunted and nodded toward the battered wooden door. So, I figured I should sit down beside him, even though the bench had this weird tilt that makes you feel like you’re sliding off, but I didn’t mention it. 

The thing is, you can almost feel the history oozing from the house, if you believe in that sort of thing. Every time I visit, I get this itch between my shoulder blades, like ghosts of old arguments or laughter or whatever, pressing in. I started, “So, um, have you—has the master been around lately, or is it just you?” I immediately regretted asking, because he shot me this look like I’d interrupted something important, even though I’m pretty sure he was just watching the clouds. 

“Master’s gone, must’ve left before the mist rolled in,” Heathcliff muttered, not really meeting my gaze. You ever have that feeling, like you’re asking the wrong question before you even finish speaking? That’s me, most of the time. And honestly, Heathcliff’s not big on details, so he just shrugs or grumbles, and I have to guess at what’s really happening. 

Anyway, we sat there for a while. I tried to remember why I thought coming to the house was a good idea, but nothing came. Birds muddled about in the yard, shadows stretched longer across the broken stones. If I’m being real, it’s a little unsettling, that emptiness, but Heathcliff seemed fine with it. I tried again, “You—you ever get tired of this place?” He didn’t answer for what felt like ages. 

“Not really,” he finally said, voice low, “Been here since before anyone can remember. It’s just a house. You get used to it.” But, uh, I’m not sure I believed him. You ever wonder how people can stay somewhere that feels sad, like the walls soak up all the joy and spit it back as cold drafts? That’s the old house, at least for me. 

I scratched at the peeling paint with my thumbnail, thinking maybe I’d say something smart, something that would, I don’t know, open him up. But all I got out was, “Looks like it’s gonna rain.” Which, by the way, was probably obvious to anyone with eyes. He smiled, a lopsided thing, and shook his head. “It always does, here.” 

Well, we just sat, letting the silence stretch until it felt kind of good, not awkward. I mean, sometimes sitting with someone, not having to fill the space with words, is the best you can do. The sky got darker, and the wind picked up, rattling the windows behind us. For a minute I thought about asking how long he’d stay, whether he ever thought about leaving, but I stopped myself. It’s not my business, really. 

There was a moment where a dog barked somewhere in the distance, and Heathcliff’s shoulders stiffened, so I was about to ask if he was alright, but then he relaxed again. Nobody came out of the house. The thing is, you learn more watching people not talk than you do listening to their stories, sometimes. Maybe that’s why I keep coming back, even though I never get real answers. 

The rain started, slow at first, then pattering down in thick sheets. Heathcliff pulled his coat tighter, and I thought about heading home, but something kept me there. “You wanna go inside?” I asked, almost without thinking. He shook his head. “Nah. Rain’s fine.” We sat together, getting wet, and for some reason I felt lighter than before. 

So the night came on, and the old house stood there, like it always does. Heathcliff stayed quiet, but I think he was glad for the company, even if neither of us said much. I guess, in the end, sometimes you don’t need to see or say anything, just sit with someone, and let the evening pass. Isn’t that enough?

Right, so I guess what I’m trying to say is, the whole business of good and evil and all that, it’s rough to figure out—especially when you’re sitting there just staring at your hands and thinking, like, is this really it, is this the life I’ve got, is there any bigger reason, or am I supposed to just, I dunno, keep going and hope for the best? And you know how some people are always talking about gods, or God, and how that’s supposed to give us some kind of direction—you know, you’re meant to do good, you’re meant to avoid bad things, and everything will be fine, or at least you’ll feel like you tried. But what if, and hear me out, what if there’s nothing really behind the curtain, no gods up there smiling down, no big scorecards for earthly stuff, just you and your choices and the stuff you can see and touch?

I mean, it sounds bleak, maybe, but it’s also kinda freeing, right? Like, if there’s no one watching except, well, people around you, then the whole game changes—and honestly, it makes being good something you actually choose instead of something you’re forced into. But then again, what does good even mean? I get that people usually talk about helping others, being fair, not messing things up too badly for anyone else, but is it really possible to know if you’re making the right choice every time? I’m not convinced it works that way. Sometimes, you can do all the “right” things and still feel like a fraud, like you’re just performing goodness because someone told you to. But without god, or gods, or whatever, isn’t the true thing just doing your best, even when nobody’s watching you and there’s no reward waiting at the end?

It’s funny, too, because once you drop all the heavenly stuff—like, seriously put it aside and just try to live on this earth—you start to see that being good is way more complicated than just following the rules. I mean, one person’s good is another person’s pain, and you end up juggling all these pieces, trying to make sense of it. Sometimes you wake up and feel like you could really make things better, maybe for your family, maybe for strangers, maybe even just for yourself, and then the day crashes in and suddenly you’re just reacting, trying to pick up the pieces. Who’s keeping score? Is there even anyone paying attention, besides maybe the bored guy in the coffee shop who watched you smile at that lost kid? Nah, mostly it’s just you, and the choices you’ve got in front of you.

So then, I guess if there’s—if there isn’t any god, or gods, and all you’ve got are the earthly things you can grab onto, maybe the game shifts; maybe what matters is making life a little bit easier for the people next to you, even if it doesn’t feel epic or grand or holy. Is it enough? That’s a question I keep coming back to. The thing is, nobody really gives you an answer, not a real one anyway. You just kinda stumble around, doing what you can, hoping that it adds up to something that feels true, even if it’s small.

And sometimes, when the night’s quiet and you’re just sitting there with your thoughts, you start asking yourself if there’s supposed to be more, if maybe everyone else knows a secret you somehow missed. But then you realize, nah, everyone’s probably just as confused, just as messy and uncertain as you. I’ve talked to people who swear there’s a purpose behind everything, that some cosmic judge is watching, and I’ve talked to people who laugh at the idea, saying it’s all just chaos and luck. Both sides have their reasons, but if I’m honest, I don’t think anybody’s got it figured out.

Anyway, I guess what I’m left with is this: doing good, whatever that means, isn’t about pleasing gods or following a map you found in a holy book—it’s about the small stuff, like making someone’s day a bit brighter, or not making things worse than they already are. It’s messy, it’s imperfect, and it definitely doesn't always feel important. But maybe that’s all you get, and maybe it’s enough.

So, here's the thing: there was this old king and—look, I know what you’re probably thinking, another king story, but just hear me out—he wasn’t just old, he was also, like, tired of everyone’s nonsense. You could see it in the way his eyes drifted off whenever someone tried to flatter him. And, uh, he had this chamberlain, old as him, maybe older, named Mr. Giles or maybe just Giles. I’m not sure anyone called him “mister” to his face, but he had that sort of groaning dignity anyway.

There was a lady called Anne who kinda floated around the edges of the hall, always in dresses that looked like they came from another time. People said she was related to someone important, I dunno, maybe the king’s cousin’s cousin or something. She had a habit of smiling at everyone like she knew some secret. I guess—well, I guess everyone thought she was nice, but maybe not good in the way chamberlain Giles was good. You know how some people just do stuff for the sake of doing good? Yeah, that was Giles, not Anne.

The palace wasn’t fancy, not how you’d imagine. The floors creaked and the tapestries had moth holes. There were mice sometimes. Okay, a lot. The king tried to pretend he didn’t notice, but Anne always looked at the skittering creatures as if she knew they might just be smarter than most of the court.

So one morning, the king woke up cranky—like, crack-of-dawn, can’t-sleep sort of cranky. He shuffled down the main stairs (carefully, because, y’know, he’s old) and said—well, sort of barked—“Where’s my chamberlain?” Giles, who’d been up before the sun, shuffled in and bowed so low it looked like his back might snap. And the king waved at him, kinda dismissive.

I mean, have you ever seen two people who trust each other so much they talk in half sentences? That was them. The king would say “The thing with the accounts—” and Giles would nod and already be heading for the treasury. No wasted words. Anne would watch from the doorway, not getting in the way, just listening. Maybe learning, I dunno.

Here’s where everything started to go weird. The thing is, Anne—see, she wasn’t content to just stand there smiling forever. One day, when the king was distracted by arguing with his cook about whether salt belonged in porridge, she drifted over to Giles and said, “Do you think the king is happy?” What do you even say to that? Giles just raised an eyebrow and said, “It’s not my place to know.”

Anne sorta laughed, soft and kind of sad. She said, “If you were king, what would you do different?” Giles shuffled his feet, looked at his shoes. I guess he’d never thought about that because he just mumbled something about “doing good is more important than being king.” Was that wise or just obvious? Who knows.

Later that night—well, it was more like evening, but it gets dark early in autumn—Anne found the king alone in the garden. He didn’t look surprised, just tired. She asked if he’d ever wanted to run away. He smiled for the first time anyone could remember, which was honestly almost unsettling. “Of course,” he said, “but who’d look after Giles?” That was the closest he got to admitting anything, I think.

So they sat there for a while. The garden wasn’t much, just some overgrown hedges and one very stubborn rosebush. Anne picked at the thorns, and the king watched her, like he was waiting for her to ask him for something. But she never did, not that night. They just listened to the wind, and maybe the mice scrabbling around in the ivy.

The next morning, everything was, I dunno, a little lighter. The king grumbled less. Giles brought out tea for two instead of just for one. Anne smiled the same way, but now it seemed more, real? Something had shifted, like, quietly. And nobody said anything about it. Maybe that’s how things change, little by little, two people at a time. Or maybe it takes more. Is that silly? Maybe. But honestly, what else is there—if not small, good things that nobody notices except two or three people, and probably some mice?

So, right, I was gonna tell you about... well, about Prospero. Yeah, that's the guy's name, and you might be thinking, "Okay, what's so special about him?" Everyone's just, I dunno, scared or maybe confused by him.

There's this wind that kicks up whenever he's annoyed. Not kidding. One minute it's dead calm, the next the palms are thrashing and there's sand in your mouth. And Ariel, you know, that weird little sprite—he's always zipping around, half-seen, half-heard, laughing when things are quiet and crying when you wish he'd just stop. Is Ariel even a "he?" Sometimes Ariel talks like a kid, sometimes all grown up. Sometimes the words don't even make sense, just rhyme after rhyme, until your own head starts spinning.

But Prospero, he's got this way of talking that makes everything sound... official, I guess. "Thou wilt do as I command," he'll say, and everybody just nods like, well, yeah, guess I will. But I've seen him talking to himself, muttering about "thee" and "thy purpose" and all this old-fashioned stuff like he swallowed a whole book and can't stop quoting it.

Oh, and there's Alonso too, who just showed up one day, looking lost. Prospero just gave him that look—you know, like, "I know everything about you, so don't even try." Alonso kept trying to explain himself, to justify why he did what he did (though I'm still not sure what that was—is anyone?), but Prospero kept cutting him off. "Yet thou hast not answered me," he'd say, and then the whole conversation would just stall while Ariel flew circles above, humming.

Some days it's quiet. The sea's just a mirror, and you can see all the way down, like there's secrets in the sand if you just stare long enough. Then there are days when Prospero decides everybody needs a lesson, and man, that's when things get weird. Storms that come out of nowhere, voices in the branches, shadows moving where there shouldn't be any. Is he just messing around, or is there a reason? Seriously, does he know something we don't, or is he just... bored?

I've tried talking to Ariel a couple of times. It's not easy. Ariel's got this habit of answering questions with more questions. Like, "Why art thou here?" or "Know'st thou what thou seekest?" And me, I'm just standing there thinking, "Uh, I don't even know what I'm supposed to be looking for, dude." Sometimes Ariel gets all serious and whispers, "All is not as it seems," and then vanishes before you can ask what that means.

And, right, Prospero. The thing is, sometimes he looks tired, you know? Like the weight of all those words, all that magic or whatever it is, is just too much. Has he always been this way? Was he ever just... normal? Maybe that's what happens when you spend too much time on your own, talking to clouds and bossing around spirits. I can't really blame him. It's a lonely place, this island.

But listen, I get the feeling none of it’s really about the magic or the storms or the weird way he talks. It’s like he’s waiting for something—someone? Or maybe just for everyone to understand what he’s been trying to say all along, buried between the "thou" and "thy" and all that. But maybe nobody ever will. I mean, how could we? We don’t have—well, whatever it is he’s got.

Do you ever wonder if people like Prospero even want to be understood? Or if they just like having secrets, holding them tight until the very end? I guess I’d ask him, but, you know, he’d probably just quote some old poem and walk away, and honestly, I’m not sure I’d understand the answer anyway.

So yeah, that's what's going on. Prospero, Ariel, Alonso, and... the ghosts, maybe. Or just the wind. Who really knows?

I mean, I guess I could blame it on the sign hanging crooked above the door, flickering so much it almost looked like Morse code, but, well, I don’t really know Morse code. Anyway, Ishmael was standing there—he was always the first one to arrive and the last to leave, not that anybody asked him to be—and he kept glancing over his shoulder like he expected something to crawl up behind him. Maybe I should’ve asked him what was wrong, but I figured he’d just shrug and mumble something about "bad energy" or whatever he calls it, so I let it go.

You ever get the feeling that a place is watching you? Like, not the people inside, but the place itself, the walls and the windows and the floor, almost like it’s got eyes and it’s just waiting for you to do something stupid? That was exactly how it felt, standing outside that battered door. The light from the sign spilled out over the sidewalk, making everything look even worse—a little bit yellow, a little bit sick, and somehow dirty. I guess that’s the best way I can put it. And, honestly, I thought about just turning around and leaving, but then Ishmael nodded at me and it was like, okay, I can’t leave him out here alone.

Once we were both inside, it was almost too quiet. You expect places like that to be noisy, but it was as if the air itself got sucked out the second the door closed. I could hear Ishmael’s breathing, which was weirdly loud, and then my own, which suddenly sounded jittery and too fast, like I was nervous for no good reason. The thing is, I don’t even get nervous usually, so what was going on? I mean, it could've been the night, or the sign, or whatever rumor I'd heard about the place a couple years back, but most likely it was just my imagination running wild again.

Ishmael went over to the counter and tapped it, probably trying to get someone’s attention, but nobody came. I noticed a faded sticker peeling off the edge—it had a cartoon bird on it, but half the image was gone, leaving just a wing and a beak that looked oddly aggressive, as if it might peck you if you touched it. I almost laughed, but Ishmael shot me a look so sharp I forgot what was even funny. He whispered, “Do you see anything?” like maybe there were clues I was missing, but all I saw was dust and scratched-up wood and the ghost of a shadow flickering under the weird light.

And, you know, I started thinking—what if nobody ever came and we were stuck here all night? Would it get colder? Would we find out why the sign was flickering, or why everybody says not to go in after midnight? Those questions were rattling around in my head like marbles in a can. Ishmael shuffled his feet and looked at the door, then looked at me, then back at the door, and I could tell he was weighing whether to say something important or just keep holding it in, like usual. He finally cleared his throat and said, “Maybe it’s closed,” but his voice broke a little, so it sounded more like he was asking rather than telling.

There was a sound from somewhere behind the counter, like maybe a bottle rolling or a foot scraping. I wondered if we should just walk out, but the sign outside was still flickering, spelling out something or nothing, and even though my common sense was screaming at me, I felt glued to the spot. Ishmael, too. We just stood there, watching the place, hoping it would blink first, almost as if it was a game we had to win. I don’t know how much time passed—could’ve been ten minutes, could’ve been an hour—but eventually Ishmael looked at me and grinned, like he’d figured something out. He said, “It’s a sign, man.” And that was all he said.

So yeah, we left. The sign was still flickering, the place was still watching, and honestly, I have no idea if it was ever open at all. I guess that’s the point sometimes, right? You go somewhere, you wait, you look, you think too much, and you walk away, only feeling like you missed something you probably never would've found anyway.

So, uh, the thing is, Richard looked every bit the part of, I dunno, some old painting you keep meaning to take off the wall but never do. He stood by the window, sort of fidgeting with his cuff, waiting for the king to come in—which, I mean, isn’t that the kind of thing that makes you sweat, no matter how many times it happens? The curtains barely moved, but he stared through them anyway, like maybe he’d catch his own reflection doing something interesting.

Duchess Anne was already there, sitting way too upright on a chair that honestly looked like it wanted to eat her. She kept glancing at Elizabeth, who was, like, not making it any easier. Elizabeth, the queen, always did this thing where she’d half-smile, half-frown, and you really couldn’t tell if you were about to get a pearl necklace or a rather heavy book chucked in your direction. You ever meet someone who could ruin your day with a single raised eyebrow? Yeah.

So, anyway, the king finally sweeps in, wearing that red velvet coat with the gold buttons—oh, and did I mention it’s way too hot for velvet? He’s grinning, but the edges of it are sharp, and everyone stands up, which is—well—just what you do, right? He looks at Richard like they’re the only two people in the room, and suddenly Richard’s all formal and even, like, bows a little, though he tries to play it off.

“Richard, thou art looking pale today,” the king says, and the whole room just freezes. You could’ve heard a pin drop—or, I don’t know, a heart breaking somewhere back in the corner. Richard kind of laughs—it’s not genuine, but what else do you do? “My liege, I—well, the morning’s been cooler than I’d thought. Or perhaps I am just missing the sun.” And the king, he sort of rolls that answer around in his mouth, as if he’s tasting it for poison.

Anne—the duchess—says nothing, because, I guess, what’s she supposed to say? She fiddles with her ring, her eyes darting. Is it just me, or does it get colder in the room when nobody talks? Finally, Elizabeth lets out this tiny, tired sigh. She looks at Richard, and it’s almost kind. “Come, sir, we’ve had little enough cheer. Wilt thou not give us a story? Something merry, or at least, not dreadful?”

Richard swallows. You can see it. He nods and glances at the fireplace, which isn’t lit, but has got enough ashes to make you wonder what burned last night. “A story, my queen? I fear I have only tired old tales. Once there was a boy who wished to be king, and—” And he stops, maybe realizing that, uh, this might be the definition of bad timing. The king, though, leans forward, curious, almost hungry.

“And did the boy become king?” The king’s voice is—how to say—like when you hear thunder way off, but you know the storm’s coming. For a second, nobody breathes. Richard manages a wobbly smile. “Aye, sire, he did. But he found no rest there. The crown sits heavier than the head can bear.”

Anne, bless her, speaks up then. Her voice is soft, but it cuts through the tension like, I dunno, really expensive butter. “But surely, to wear the crown is to have the world, is it not? Or do I misremember my own stories?” Again, that quiet. Even the dust seems to settle in for the response. The king’s eyes move from Anne to Richard, and back again. “The world, aye, Duchess. But what is the world, if not full of thorns?” He says it like he’s quoting someone, or maybe just himself.

Elizabeth stands then, because she’s the queen and she can do what she wants. “Come, this is all too grim,” she says, and for some reason, everyone almost laughs with relief. “Let us walk in the gardens. The roses have come in at last—and, if thou wilt, Richard, we’ll have no more sad tales until supper.”

And that’s how it goes, right? You try to keep things light, but old stories creep in anyway. Does anybody really know what people are thinking in those rooms? I mean, with all the titles and the velvet and the impossible smiles? I sure don’t. And honestly, sometimes it’s the silences that tell you more than the words ever could.

You know, I never really thought I'd end up at Wuthering Hall on a Thursday afternoon, but that's just how things go sometimes, right? The thing is, when Linton sent that weirdly formal invitation, I figured, okay, it's probably just a tea or something. But then Edgar showed up, and he had this look like he'd accidentally walked into a midterm exam and, uh, I guess Heathcliff was already there in the corner, looking like he was about to swallow a thundercloud or two. So, I mean, what was I supposed to do? Pretend it was normal?

There's this awkward silence, broken only by Linton fussing with some tea things, and Edgar chewing his lip, which, honestly, he does way more than anyone I've met. Heathcliff just watched us all, not blinking, like he's waiting for somebody (maybe one of us) to slip up. Would you have done something? I kind of wish I'd just made up an excuse and left, but, well, I stayed.

"So, um, shall we sit?" Linton asked, except he said it like he wasn't sure if he really wanted us to, or if he was just, I dunno, filling space. He put his teacup down, and it clattered, and everyone's nerves just spiked a notch.

Heathcliff finally moved, pulling out a chair for himself, not bothering with any of the niceties. I think Edgar tried to say something—his mouth opened, but nothing came out except this tiny cough, and then he looked at his feet. The whole thing felt like a set-up, like there was something we weren't told, y'know? So I just tried to keep quiet, but my foot kicked Linton's under the table and—well, that didn't help anything. He glared, and I mumbled an apology, which Edgar repeated back even though he had nothing to do with it.

"So," Heathcliff said finally, his voice gravelly, "I suppose we're all waiting for someone to get to the point."

Linton gave this nervous giggle, and Edgar stammered, "Well, I—I thought, um, perhaps we could, you know, sort things out?"

"Sort what out?" Heathcliff's eyebrows went up like he hadn't heard anything more ridiculous all week, and, honestly, I couldn't blame him. I hadn't a clue either.

Edgar straightened, and his voice got stronger, kind of. "Linton, maybe you'd like to say, uh, what it is we should... wish for?"

Now, I know that sounds kind of weird, but trust me, Edgar's always worrying about people's intentions. Linton tugged at his sleeve, thinking, and finally blurted, "I just... I wanted to get everyone together. One time. Like, maybe... mending things?"

Would anyone have guessed that's what he was after? Not me. Heathcliff snorted, and Edgar frowned so hard I thought he'd crack his own forehead. Me, I figured, hey, sometimes you gotta try, even if it turns messy.

Heathcliff leaned in, elbows on the table, and said, "You wish for peace, then? Between us all?"

Linton swallowed, hard. "Yes. If we could—just for a day—not argue, not fight... That would mean everything to me."

The thing is, nobody answered right away. It was just the wind whistling outside and, you know, Linton with his hopeful eyes darting around. Edgar finally nodded, but it was more like he was agreeing to something unpleasant, not a party. Heathcliff looked at him, then at Linton, and just shrugged.

"I can stay quiet," he said, "if that's what you want. But don’t expect miracles."

Edgar exhaled and said, "Well, that's as good as we'll get."

And then, for a weird moment, we all sat there, sipping lukewarm tea and pretending not to notice how uncomfortable it was. I wish I could say something changed, like a switch flipping, but, nah, we just managed not to yell for a bit, and sometimes that's enough. Linton smiled, small and tentative, and Edgar softened a little, and Heathcliff—well, he didn't storm off.

So, what do you think? Is it really possible to get people together and make them see eye to eye? Maybe, maybe not. But, anyway, we all left the hall that afternoon, and I think, for once, nobody looked back with regret. Or, at least, that's what I hope.
