So, look, the thing is, I don't know if you've ever wandered into the woods at night, but it's not great for clear thinking. I mean, maybe you think you can handle it, but then the moon does this weird thing with the shadows, and suddenly every tree is—well, it's not just a tree anymore. It's some kind of, I don't know, like, guardian or trickster or, sometimes, just an old friend. Or maybe that's just me. Anyway, it was one of those humid nights where you can't really tell if the sweat on your skin is yours or if the air's just clinging to you.

So that's how I ended up, chest thumping, squinting between branches, and trying to figure out where Demetrius went. He'd said he'd be back quick. He never is, honestly, but I still waited. The frogs were loud. I tried counting the croaks but I kept losing my place, like, what's the point, right? So I was sitting on this half-rotten log and kicking at a patch of moss, thinking about Hermia. If I was being fair, I guess I was mostly trying not to think about Hermia. But, well, you know how that goes.

Then there was this flicker, not really a light, more like a small movement that your brain tries to make sense of, except it can't. I said, "Who's there?" and meant it to sound confident, but it came out kind of squeaky. Silence. Then a giggle. Is there anything worse than hearing a giggle in the forest when you're alone? I don't think so. I jumped up, almost fell over, and turned in a full circle like I was gonna spot something important.

"Show yourself," I said, and wished I hadn't.

A rustle to my left, and there's Puck. Not like, capital Puck, legendary mischief guy—well, okay, actually, sort of that exactly. He was leaning against a birch, picking at his nails. He had that look like he knew how the next five minutes would go, and, honestly, maybe the next five years.

"You lost?" he said, all casual, like people just appear in forests at midnight all the time.

"I'm not lost," I said, because that's what people say, even when they're lying. "I'm waiting for someone." Which felt like another lie as soon as I said it, but you can't take those back.

He grinned. "You humans are funny. Always so sure you know who you want, right up until the moon changes or—" He made this little gesture, like flicking dust from his fingers. "Or something else does."

"Where's Demetrius?" I asked, trying to sound bored. I don't think I managed it.

Puck tipped his head, eyes shining. "He wants Hermia, you want Hermia, Hermia wants—" He shrugged. "Who knows?"

"That's not true," I said, but even to me it sounded wrong. I kicked the moss again. The feeling in my chest was, like, tight. "If thou knowest everything, then what am I supposed to do?"

He laughed, but it wasn't mean. "Why ask me? I'm just the one who stirs things up. Choices are for you. Unless you want help." He squinted. "Do you?"

Did I? I tried to picture it, Puck fixing my life with a snap of his fingers: Demetrius suddenly forgetting Hermia, Hermia turning and seeing me. Would that even feel right? Isn't half the wanting wrapped up in the not having?

I shook my head. "It's not that simple," I muttered.

"Ah, but nothing true ever is," he said, and then he was gone. Not with a bang or a dramatic flash, just—gone. Which is maybe worse.

I stood there, and I guess I waited. Maybe for Demetrius, maybe for Hermia, maybe for nothing at all. The night pressed in, thick and warm, and there were more laughs—soft, like leaves, maybe just the wind, maybe not. If you were there, you might've heard me ask, real quiet, "What do I look like to you?" but no one answered.

And that's how it goes, right? You think you know what you want, you chase after it, and in the dark, sometimes, you find yourself asking questions no one can answer. Or, I mean, maybe that's just me.

So, yeah, I mean—look, it’s late and you probably just want the story, but the thing is: I can’t really remember how it started. It’s fuzzy. Was it raining? Maybe. Or maybe it was sunny and I’m just mixing it up with another afternoon. There’s this pub, right, over by the river where the old bridge used to be, and everyone always talks about the food—like, it’s got the best leeks in soup in town. That’s a weird thing to be famous for, but, hey, people still come in droves.

Okay, I’ll get to the point. Fluellen’s working behind the bar, trying to look busy, but he’s got this vibe, y’know, like he’s the only good guy in the joint. He’s wiping the counter—some sticky stuff, don’t ask me what, and muttering about how no one appreciates a proper leek. “Leek’s a good vegetable,” he says to nobody in particular. I mean, is it? I don’t know. I just eat whatever’s in front of me. But Fluellen’s got beef about it, thinks people should pray for the leek at dinner, not just wolf it down. He’s got this big Welsh pride about it, too, which is cool and all, but, honestly, does anyone even care?

There’s this knave—I swear, that’s the best word for him—lurking at the end of the bar. He’s got a pistol tucked under his coat and, yeah, I saw him flash it when he thought no one was looking. But Fluellen saw it, too, because that guy misses nothing. The knave’s got a face you wanna punch, but you don’t, because he also looks like he’d bite. So, anyway, the knave orders some food, asks Fluellen for the “French stuff,” which, I guess, means fries or something fancier. Fluellen just gives him the look, y’know, like he’s about to drop him through the floor.

I’m sitting there, eating—no, more like picking at my food, because, honestly, I don’t know if it’s worth the effort. The leek’s alright. It’s green. It tastes like...well, like a leek. But I nod anyway when Fluellen asks if it’s good, because why not. I don’t wanna mess with him, not tonight. He’s got that tired energy. You ever see someone who looks like they’re holding the whole world up by themselves? That’s him.

The knave gets twitchy, starts yammering about something in French that I don’t understand, maybe cursing or maybe just asking for a drink. Fluellen ignores him, gets all worked up and starts on about how people should eat more leeks and respect their roots. I mean, really, who cares about leeks? Is anyone actually listening? Well, I’m half-listening, but mostly because I don’t want to miss the moment the pistol comes out. It’s stupid, but you get bored and start expecting drama.

Suddenly, the knave stands up—way too fast, chair scraping—and everyone goes quiet. He’s got that wild look, like he’s about to do something dumb. He shouts, “Pray for your French food, you fools!” and—I mean, what?—he sounds insane. Fluellen doesn’t flinch, just walks over and puts his hand out. I’m thinking, is this the part where someone gets shot? But nope, Fluellen just tugs the knave’s coat until the pistol falls out. It’s not even loaded, turns out. The knave looks even smaller, somehow, once he’s lost the pistol.

“Eat your leek,” Fluellen says, pushing a bowl in front of him. The knave hesitates, glances at me, like I’m gonna help him. I shrug. Eat your leek, man. The world’s rough, but you gotta eat.

So, the knave slumps down and starts eating, mumbling in French—maybe about how leeks aren’t so bad, maybe about wanting to go home. Fluellen’s got this calm thing going now, wiping the bar again, saying, “Good food makes good people.” Nobody knows what that really means, but it sounds nice. I finish my soup, which tastes better suddenly—not sure why. Maybe it’s just relief.

I mean, what makes a pub safe? Is it the food, or is it the people who care enough to stand up even when things get weird? Fluellen’s still working, smiling a bit, and everyone starts talking again, like nothing happened.

So yeah, that’s it, I guess. Leek soup, a knave, a pistol, and a little bit of French.

So, look, here's what happened—or, well, here's how I remember it, which is probably not exactly how it went down, alright? The thing is, the room was stuffy and kind of cluttered, but in the way that makes you think someone actually lives there, not like those magazine rooms where you wonder if anybody ever drops a crumb. Anyway, Porfiry was standing by the only window, and honestly, he just looked tired. Not, like, physically tired, more like he'd been thinking too much. You know how your brain gets all fogged up? It was like that. He didn't even turn around when I came in.

"So, you came," he said, and he let out this little sigh. I couldn't tell if he was annoyed or just bored. Maybe both, but who knows?

I shuffled my feet—yeah, I know, super confident—and said, "Well, you wanted to talk, didn't you?" Like I wasn't the one who'd been waiting ten minutes in the hallway, pretending to read a grocery list hanging on the wall. The man didn't laugh, just nodded like, yeah, okay, let's get this over with.

Porfiry finally looked at me, and I swear, his eyes had this way of making you feel like he was seeing past all your usual nonsense. "Sit down," he said. So I sat, even though the chair squeaked like it was gonna collapse. You ever wonder why the most uncomfortable chairs always end up in the rooms where you have to have real conversations?

He started talking, sort of slow, like he was choosing his words. "People say things, you know? They talk about what's happened, and what could have happened, and what should've happened," he began. "But I'm asking you—what did happen? That's what matters." He stared so hard it almost hurt.

I didn't know what to say right away. I looked at the floor, counted the cracks in the wood. It's funny, the things you notice when you don't want to answer a question. "I dunno," I finally muttered. "I was there, I guess. I mean—I saw some of it. Not all."

He leaned back and folded his arms. His jacket was too big for him, hung off his shoulders like it belonged to someone else. "You saw some of it," he repeated, but softer this time. "But what did you do?"

That got me. What did I do? I mean, that's the thing, right? Everyone acts like there's some clear line, like you either did a thing or you didn't, but life's messier than that. I opened my mouth and then closed it again, 'cause—well, what was I supposed to say? Sometimes a thing just happens and you're there, and then people want you to explain every little detail, like you can just roll it back in your head and pick it apart.

Porfiry didn't push. He just waited. That was his whole thing, really. He waited until you tripped over your own thoughts and accidentally said something true.

"I...I wasn't sure what was going on," I said, and that much was real. "It happened so fast. I heard someone shout, and then... I don't know, I guess I froze. I couldn't—" I cut myself off. Why was it so hard to say? "I couldn't move."

He nodded, like he'd expected that. Like, maybe he's heard it a hundred times before. He got up and went over to this old cabinet, rummaged around a bit, then pulled out a chipped mug. Poured us both tea, kind that smells stronger than it tastes. Handed me one and sat back down.

"You ever think about what you'd do if you could go back?" Porfiry asked, and this time his voice was quieter. Not sad, exactly, just... I dunno, faded. Like he'd asked himself the same thing lots of times and never got a good answer.

I looked at him, and for a second, I almost lied. Said I'd have been braver, or whatever. But the truth was, I didn't know. I took a sip of tea and stared out the window at the rooftops, all gray and close together. "I think about it all the time," I said. "But it doesn't change anything, does it?"

Porfiry just smiled in that tired way, and the room got quiet, except for the sound of old pipes somewhere in the walls. What are you supposed to do, really, when the only witness you have is yourself? It felt like there was a lot more to say, but neither of us could figure out how to say it. So we just sat there, drinking tea, and let the silence fill in the rest.

So, I thought I’d write this out, just to get things straight, because honestly, I haven’t got anyone to talk to who’d really understand, and I’m starting to feel like I might explode if I don’t just, you know, put it somewhere. You ever get that feeling? Like your head’s so full of thoughts you could just scream? Anyway, I guess this is sorta like a letter—though it’s not really for anybody in particular, and, well, I’m not sure if it’d matter if it was.

The thing is, two months ago—yeah, it’s been that long—I started thinking a lot about god, or, I guess, whatever people believe god is. Which is weird for me, because I don’t usually get all, you know, spiritual or philosophical or anything. I mean, I grew up hearing a bunch of stuff about god and church and “doing the right thing,” but I always felt kinda skeptical, like, who decides what that even means? And honestly, nobody’s ever given me a real answer. Still, when you’re alone and time starts dragging, your mind just goes places. Maybe it’s boredom, maybe it’s something else. Who knows?

So, I found myself writing a letter that I never sent—yeah, I do that, write letters to people or things or whatever, just to make sense of my mess. This one was to god, though I didn’t really know what I wanted to say, and I definitely didn’t know what I wanted back. Which brings me to the question: if you could talk to god, what would you ask? Or maybe—what would you want to know?

I wrote about needing clarity, about wanting answers, but mostly about wanting to feel like I mattered. That sounds cheesy, I know, but after one of those days where you drop your keys, lose your phone, spill coffee all over your shirt and get yelled at for something you didn’t do, you kinda start wondering if anybody’s out there listening, or if you’re just talking to yourself.

Months slipped by, and nothing changed, really. Well, except I started paying attention to stuff I used to ignore, like little lessons. You know, things you pick up when you’re forced to sit still—like how the neighbor’s dog barks at exactly 6:07 every single morning, or how the sun hits the kitchen table just right for about fourteen minutes, which, for some reason, made me think of childhood breakfasts and my dad’s terrible jokes. I think there are lessons everywhere, but they’re not spelled out, not written down like “here’s what you need to know”—they’re just, I dunno, floating there, waiting. Is that how life works? Like, you gotta pay attention or you miss everything?

Anyway, the letter stayed in my drawer. I kept adding stuff to it—random questions, half-thoughts, apologies, jokes that would make no sense to anyone but me. I even wrote, “If you’re reading this, I hope you think I’m funny,” which might be the most desperate thing I’ve ever scribbled, but who cares? Maybe god likes jokes.

And then, I realized I wasn’t all that interested in answers. I mean, sure, I wanted them, but wanting and needing are different. Over time, I just wanted connection. Like, the act of writing itself made me feel less alone, even if the only person reading was me. Maybe that’s what everyone’s after—connection, not answers.

Sometimes, when I’m sitting around waiting for the bus, or trying to fall asleep, I wonder if anyone else does this—writes stupid letters to nobody, hopes someone, or something, will care. I have friends, but I don’t talk to them about this stuff. They’d probably laugh or tell me to get over myself. That’s fine, I guess. Everybody’s got their own stuff.

So, I don’t really know what god is now. I thought I’d know after two months, or at least understand something more, but I honestly don’t. Maybe god’s just an idea, or a hope, or maybe god’s the lessons you notice when you finally stop to pay attention. Or, maybe, god’s just the feeling you get when you’re writing letters to nobody and still feel seen, somehow. I know that’s not an answer, but it’s what I got.

All I know is, I’ll keep writing. Maybe next time I’ll send a letter, or maybe I’ll just keep tossing them in drawers, and that’ll be enough. That’s the thing about wanting—you never really stop, but maybe you start wanting different things. Fewer answers, more connection. Less noise, more quiet. And, who knows, maybe that’s what god was trying to teach me all along.

So, here’s the thing, and I know it sounds like one of those stories that maybe you’ve heard a million times, but—yeah, no, trust me, you haven’t. Not like this, anyway. We’re in a city that’s loud at night and feels too quiet during the day, and you can’t walk two blocks without tripping over someone else’s drama. At the center, there’s Desdemona. She’s got this way about her that makes people want to confide their secrets, even though she’s just as likely to lose them or, you know, laugh them off with that weird half-smile she does when she’s nervous.

Okay, hang on, I’m getting ahead of myself already. Othello, he’s—well, he’s way taller than you’d expect, and there’s something always going on behind his eyes, like he’s thinking two, three steps ahead. Except, sometimes, he misses what’s right in front of him. That’s what Emilia says, anyway. And honestly, Emilia knows more than all of us, but she acts like she’s got nothing to say until she’s ready to drop a truth bomb in the middle of a conversation. How does she do that?

Anyway, one afternoon, when the sun was making everything feel sticky, Desdemona’s sitting outside this little café with Iago—yeah, that guy, always lurking like he’s got dirt on everyone. He’s playing with a coin, spinning it on the table, not even looking at her, just tossing out these random comments about trust and—well, betrayal, basically. Desdemona’s mostly ignoring him, humming to herself, twisting her ring around her finger, but you can tell she’s actually listening. I mean, why wouldn’t she? The way Iago says things, it’s like he knows you better than you know yourself.

Iago grins, real slow, and says, “If Othello were here, d’you think he’d notice if you left?” Which is, honestly, kind of a mean thing to say but also exactly the kind of thing you gotta wonder about. And Desdemona frowns—shrugs—and says, “He’d notice. I think he would. I hope so.” But she sounds a little less sure at the end there, and Iago leans back in his chair, looking all satisfied, like he’s just proven something.

Then, out of nowhere, the Clown walks by—yeah, we have a clown, but not the funny kind, more like the wandering-joke kind that’s, you know, mostly jokes at your expense. He stops, makes a show of pretending he’s lost, asks if anyone’s seen his left shoe. Desdemona laughs, actually laughs, which you’d think would break up the tension, but somehow it just makes it worse.

Iago, of course, jumps on that, says, “You laugh easily, my lady. Wish I could say the same for your husband.” And Desdemona’s face goes all tight, and for a second it’s like no one’s breathing, not even the people at the next table. Emilia’s there now, too—she just appears, like she does—and she puts a hand on Desdemona’s shoulder, real gentle. “Let’s go,” she says. “You don’t have to sit here and listen to this.”

Desdemona hesitates, looking at the table, at her hands, at the bit of pastry she hasn’t even touched. “I just wanted to feel normal,” she mumbles, which is not what anyone expects her to say. Iago snorts, but Emilia glares at him, and says, “Let’s walk,” and finally Desdemona stands up and follows her.

So they’re on the street, and Emilia’s talking, low and steady, about how sometimes love is just a mess you gotta sort through with your eyes closed. Desdemona listens, nods, maybe half-believes it. There’s a dog barking somewhere, and the city smells like coffee and something burning, and in that moment, Desdemona looks at Emilia and whispers, “Do you think he really knows me?” Like, really, how do you ever know what someone’s thinking, even when you want to trust them?

Emilia squeezes her hand and says, “You’re more than your worries, Des. He’s just a man.” Which, coming from Emilia, sounds like both a comfort and a warning.

And then—well, life goes on, I guess. Othello’s probably waiting at home, maybe wondering where she is, maybe not. The Clown finds his shoe, or doesn’t, and Iago keeps spinning his coins, stirring up more trouble when he gets bored. And Desdemona? She keeps walking, hand in hand

So, the thing is, Jessica had never planned to leave the old house in the first place—well, that's not entirely true, but you know what I mean. She was always saying stuff like, "I'm stuck here," and mumbling about her dad, but you could see the way she'd look out the window and sigh, especially when Launcelet was hanging around, doing his usual tricks and telling her about the streets outside. And honestly, you can't blame her; who wouldn't want to get out after years of listening to Shylock muttering about coins or how the world's out to get him?

One time, I overheard her talking to Lorenzo, though it was barely more than whispers. She was like, "Shall we go tonight?" and he was all nervous, but then tried to laugh it off—only it didn't really sound like a laugh, you know? Anyway, I couldn't tell if she actually meant it right then, or if it was just one of those things you say when you're scared and excited all at once. And isn't that how most plans start? You say something wild, then wonder if you'll ever actually do it.

So, that night, she waited by the window—watching for the signal, I guess. The moon was out and everything looked kind of magical, though the city wasn't exactly quiet. I think she was scared her father would catch her, but he was so busy counting money, he barely noticed anything outside his little circles. Launcelet kept pacing near the door; he was supposed to help, but honestly, he just made everything more tense.

Okay, look, I know nobody expects these things to go smooth. There's always something. This time, Gratiano was supposed to distract Shylock. He's got that loud voice and he's always laughing, so he thought he'd keep the old man busy. But do you think it worked? Nope. Shylock wouldn't budge; he kept demanding everyone be quiet, going on about "thou shalt respect this house," which, frankly, he said almost every day.

Jessica hesitated, even though she'd packed her little bag and put on her cloak. I'm pretty sure she was shaking. Lorenzo stood in the shadows, waiting for his cue. If you could've seen them, you'd think, "Why risk it?" But isn't it true that sometimes people do crazy things for love, or maybe just to feel free for once?

And then, just as Launcelet whispered, "Go now," Jessica slipped out. She did it so quick, you might've missed it. Shylock yelled out from inside, but instantly Lorenzo and Gratiano started shouting too, all in different directions, and for a minute nobody knew who was where. I heard someone drop something; it sounded like a coin but maybe it was just keys. Anyway, Jessica kept moving, even though her heart was pounding so loud I bet she thought everyone could hear it.

Honestly, I didn’t think she’d make it. Shylock was right behind her, shouting about betrayal and oaths and all that stuff he never stopped obsessing over. But Jessica wasn’t stopping—she ran right past the gate and into Lorenzo’s arms. He smiled, a real smile, not one of those fake ones. Like, you could see relief all over him.

For a second, everything went quiet. I mean, you could almost feel the pause in the air. Then Gratiano started laughing again, and Launcelet just wiped his brow like he’d finished a marathon. Jessica finally took a breath, and the thing is, she looked up at Lorenzo like she was seeing daylight for the first time. I wondered, does running away always feel this wild, or is it just her?

They walked off together, but nobody was sure what would happen next. Would Shylock hunt them down? Would she regret leaving? I guess you can’t really know until you’re the one standing in the street, holding someone’s hand and trusting you made the right move. Maybe it’s not about being Christian or anything like that—maybe it’s just wanting to belong somewhere, to someone, without all the old shadows hanging over you.

And if you ask me, Jessica wasn’t running from her father, not really. She was running towards herself, or at least the idea of who she could be. Isn’t that what we’re all trying to do, in the end? So there they went, under the moon, uncertain but together, and I watched until they disappeared.

So, I guess I should just start at the point where everything kind of went sideways, though to be honest, with us it always went sideways at some point, didn't it? We were a pretty ragtag bunch of friends, stitched together more by, I dunno, time and some shared history than anything else—like, nobody would pick us out in a crowd and think, "Oh, there go the best of chums," not by a long shot. Still, when Paul came staggering into the old café all flushed and out of breath that one rainy Thursday, even old Jules—who barely looked up from his paper most days—couldn't help but raise his eyebrows and say, in that kind of grumpy french way of his, "Qu'est-ce qui se passe, mon ami?" which just means "What's up?" but it sounds fancier.

Paul, well, he's the sort of man you want to believe—tall, got that honest look about him, though if you'd asked me last year, I'd have said he's always a bit too quick to buy some wild story. Anyway, that day he drops his umbrella, nearly takes out my espresso, and blurts out something about losing his job and, well, not just any job but his grandfather's old print shop, which he tried to keep running for the last, what, five years or so? The thing is, we all knew it was a miracle it lasted that long. We all told him to cut his losses, move on, but that's not the sort of thing Paul could ever do. Loyalty's a kind of curse for the unfortunate, if you ask me.

And honestly, I didn't know what to say. I looked to Jules, then to Greta—who was at that ancient game of pretending not to listen while she eavesdropped on the whole thing. She'd always said the shop was doomed, but she liked Paul, maybe more than she let on, and she surprised us all by reaching over, patting his hand, and saying, "We'll figure something out, won't we?" And maybe that's the moment when—look, does every group of friends have that one crisis when you just decide to dig your heels in and help, even if you know, deep down, you're fighting a losing battle? Or is that just the movies?

But anyway, we became a sort of makeshift committee right there. Jules, who hadn't moved faster than a tortoise since the Mitterrand era, offered up an ancient rolodex with names of "kind people, maybe, who remember your grand-père," though his handwriting was so bad that Paul couldn't read half the names. Greta said she'd bake and organize "some kind of fancy french fête," though she didn't know the first thing about actual baking, and I volunteered to redesign the window display, which, in hindsight, was not exactly the lifeboat you'd want in a storm—I'm more the talking sort, not the doing sort.

Days turned into a kind of strange routine—Paul moping, Jules muttering, Greta covered in flour, me fussing with colored paper and string in the dusty front window. Neighbors started popping in with this awkward blend of pity and forced cheerfulness, and, well, I suppose that's humanity for you: sometimes people don't know how to help so they bring you a basil plant or a six-pack, and maybe that does help, sort of. Sometimes the old men who hung around the square, who remembered Paul's grandfather, would come in and tell stories in a mix of French and, well, a kind of local slang that's half poetry and half nonsense.

Did it work? I wish I could say we saved the shop, pulled off a miracle, but life doesn't always hand you those clean happy endings, you know? In the end, Paul packed up the last of the type cases while we just stood there, all of us suddenly aware of how quiet it was without the old presses clattering. Jules raised his cup—wine, not coffee—and said, "To the unfortunate, and the very kind." Greta cried, of course, but that's all right. We left together, a little closer than before, I think.

And I guess that's what you get, in the end. Not what you hoped for, but each other—if you're lucky.

So look, you’d think a man wouldn’t be so easy to spot in a crowd, but I could see him before he even noticed me. His coat was—well, actually, I’m not really sure what kind of coat it was, sort of gray and way too big for his frame, hanging awkwardly like he borrowed it from a much larger friend and forgot to give it back. He had this way about him, you know, like someone who’s always searching for a lost coin or maybe waiting for a headache to pass. His eyes kept flickering around, not quite settling on anyone or anything.

And I mean, the thing is, I’ve seen that look before. It’s the look of someone who’s trying to find a reason to keep walking. Or maybe to turn back. Who really knows. I wanted to ask him where he was headed, but I didn’t. I just watched. I’m not sure why. Maybe I was curious, or maybe I thought I’d see something important, but all I saw was the way he moved—slow, shaky. He wasn’t old, not really, but there was something tired about him, like life had wrung him out and left him damp on the line.

He caught my eye for a second. Just a moment. I almost looked away, but—I didn’t. I nodded, kinda awkward, forehead heavy, and he nodded back. There’s this thing that happens when you lock eyes with someone like that. You know, you get that weird, prickly sense that you’re in on some secret together, even if you don’t know what the secret is. Like you’re both just pretending not to fall apart.

He started to walk my way, boots scraping the street, slow but still, like he wasn’t really sure where his feet were taking him. I thought about what to say. “Hey, are you okay?” Too direct, maybe. Or “Nice coat,” which would’ve been a lie, honestly, but it might’ve broken whatever silent spell hung in the air between us.

He stopped about two feet from me, and up close, I could see how pale he was. Cheeks hollow, stubble patchy like he hadn’t bothered with a mirror in days. “You got the time?” he asked, voice raspy, like he hadn’t used it in a while.

I checked, though I didn’t really need to. “Seven-thirty,” I said.

He nodded, like that meant more than it did. Then he looked past me, like he was expecting someone else to appear from behind my shoulder. I half-turned, but there was nothing—just the usual city street, people passing, tired neon.

“What’s your name?” he asked, sudden.

Now, I wasn’t ready for that. Who asks for a name anymore? I hesitated. “Mike,” I said, before I could think of a better one. Wasn’t even my name, but I didn’t want to give it. He nodded, accepting the lie like maybe he was expecting something fake. Maybe he needed it, or maybe he saw through it. Who knows.

He kept looking back down the street, shifting from foot to foot like he was waiting for something—someone. It felt like we were both just killing time, but his kind of waiting felt heavier, you know?

“Waiting for somebody?” I finally asked, just to fill the space.

He laughed, and honestly, it was the saddest thing I’ve heard in a long time. “You could say that,” he said. “But I don’t think they’re coming.”

I didn’t really know what to say. So I just stood there, hands in my pockets, and tried to figure out if I was supposed to follow, or just go. He didn’t move, though, just kept standing, hunched up, eyes flicking around. I caught him glancing at me, and for a second I wondered—what did he see? Did I look as lost as he did?

There was a kind of weakness in the way he kept holding himself up, like his arms were too heavy for his shoulders. But he was still standing. Still moving, even if it was just barely.

After a while, he sighed, dry and thin, and said, “Well, thanks, Mike.” He started to walk away, small steps, shoulders hunched, getting swallowed by the crowd. I watched him go, not sure what any of it meant, or if it was supposed to mean something. Isn’t it strange, how sometimes you see someone and you just know you’ll remember the look in their eyes for a long time? Even if you never see them again?

So, okay, here’s what happened with Lucentio—that guy’s always got something up his sleeve. He burst into the courtyard like he’d just heard the king himself was waiting, and poor Biondello nearly tripped over his own feet, trying to follow. I mean, have you ever seen someone so jumpy and at the same time, like, trying to look cool? That’s Biondello for you. He kept tugging at his cap, glancing left and right like he expected someone to drag him off any second. But really, who would care about a servant in this part of town, right?

So anyway, Lucentio grabs him by the elbow—you know, the way someone does when they want to look all serious—and says, “Biondello, you must do something for me, and you must not mess it up.” And Biondello just nods, nods, nods, even before he knows what’s being asked. Hah, good old Biondello, never says no. Is it loyalty or fear? I honestly can’t tell sometimes.

But here’s the thing: Lucentio’s got his eyes on Baptista’s daughter, Katherina. Or, wait, no, no, it’s the younger one he wants—Bianca. See? Even I get mixed up, because all these fathers with their rules and lists of who can marry whom and how much money’s involved—it’s enough to scramble anyone’s brain. And so Baptista, he’s the father, and he’s so proud of his daughters that he can hardly see straight. Thinks he’s the wisest man in Padua, I bet.

So Lucentio’s got a plan, of course. He always does. He says he’ll pretend to be a tutor to get close to Bianca. Can you imagine trying to act like a teacher when your head’s full of, like, hearts and sighs and probably bad poetry? Biondello’s not sure it’ll work, but he’s not stupid enough to say that out loud. You can see it all over his face, though.

And now I guess—well, Lucentio says, “You must go to Baptista’s house and tell him that I, uh, I mean, your master, am a…what did he say? Oh, a scholar from Pisa, come to teach Latin and Greek. Make it sound grand, Biondello. Don’t stutter.” The thing is, Biondello always stutters when he’s nervous. But off he goes, tying his old coat a bit tighter and muttering to himself.

Me? I hung back, pretending to sweep stones off the path just in case anyone asked what I was doing there. But, honestly, I just wanted to see how it all turned out. Wouldn’t you? It’s not like folks fall in love and plot schemes every day around here, though sometimes it feels like it.

I watched Biondello knock at Baptista’s big wooden door, you know, the one with the lion’s head knocker that looks like it’s about to roar? For a second I thought he’d drop dead from nerves, but he managed to get through the speech, more or less. Baptista listened, arms crossed, long white beard twitching. While this was happening, Baptista’s youngest, Bianca, peeked down from the window—just a tiny bit of her face, but enough. Lucentio, who’d snuck around the corner by then, caught her eye. You know that look when two people see each other and the world basically stops? It was kind of like that, only a lot more awkward because her father was right there and poor Lucentio had chalk dust on his sleeve.

Anyway, the conversation took forever. Baptista kept asking questions, like, “Who sent you?” and “Why should I trust some traveling scholar with my daughter’s education?” and Biondello was starting to sweat. I almost wanted to run up and help, but, yeah right, who’d listen to me? At last, though, Baptista agreed to let Lucentio, “the fine scholar from Pisa,” give lessons.

So, everything’s set, at least for now. But tell me, do you really think love ever goes as planned? And why do people always assume fathers know best, anyway? The sun was already slipping behind the rooftops when Lucentio grinned at Biondello and promised him a gold coin—no idea if he’ll ever get it. But the air smelled hopeful, or maybe just like new trouble about to begin. Either way, I couldn’t help but smile as I picked up my broom and moved on.

The thing is, I always thought I could see pretty much everything from my window—like, the street, folks coming and going, the way light looked different every hour, and honestly, even the tired faces of people just trying to get home. But yesterday was weird. I don’t know if you’ve ever had one of those days where every little thing feels out of place, but, I mean, it was like that for me. I kept looking out, trying to just read the signs, you know, not literal signs but more like, what’s happening, what’s in the air. And I could see Dean out there—well, I’m assuming it was him, but maybe not, since every time I waved, whoever it was kinda just turned away or pretended not to notice.

I’d been sitting with a book in my hand, but I couldn’t really focus, so I kept flicking my eyes up. The light was going all gold and soft, but it kept slipping away behind the clouds, and every time it did, the street looked another shade darker, like someone was messing with a dimmer switch for fun. I don’t know, it felt like the world was holding its breath. Or maybe I was. Sometimes I wonder if I make all this up in my head. Like, maybe nothing actually changes, and I’m just reading stories into light and shadows 'cause I’m bored.

But anyway, Dean—or the guy I thought was Dean—was walking real slow, as if he was thinking hard about something. He stopped right near the old bench, which, by the way, I don’t think anyone’s used since last summer, and he ran his hand over the worn wood. Was he looking for something? Or maybe he just wanted to feel how rough it was under his fingers for whatever reason. The thing is, I've never really talked to Dean much, only seen him around. He’s got this way of moving, sometimes, like he’s trying to keep everything at arm’s length. I could see his face twist up for a second, then smooth out, like he caught himself feeling sad and decided to stop.

You ever feel like you wish you could just ask someone what’s up, but you sorta can’t? Or maybe you’re worried you really don’t wanna know the answer. I sat there, just holding my book, not reading a word, feeling every second stretch out like taffy. My hand was cramped from gripping the pages, and I realized I wasn’t even looking at the words anymore. Instead, I was kinda counting how many cars passed, and every time the afternoon light flickered, it felt important somehow. I mean, I started to think about all the people who’d ever walked down that street, like every step added up and maybe meant something.

Dean (okay, I’m just gonna call him that whether it was him or not) finally sat down on the bench. He took something out of his pocket, held it up to the light, then put it away quick. I couldn’t see what it was, but the way he stared at it made me kinda nervous, like maybe it was bad news or something personal. He looked around, but not at my window, and then just sat with his head in his hands. At that point, I wanted to shout out, ask if he was alright, but—well, I’m not the kind of person who does that.

I kept telling myself I’d go outside, just walk by, maybe say hello, or I don’t know, act like I dropped something and needed help. But I didn’t. Instead I just watched. I was so sure he’d get up and leave, but he didn’t. The street went quiet, the light faded until only the streetlamp was on, and I could hear my own breathing, louder than usual.

Why do people keep so much bottled up? Is it just habit, or are we all scared someone's gonna laugh if we say something real? Every night when I see someone out there, I think about reaching out, but I always end up staying put, reading another line in my book, even if I don’t remember a thing I read. And honestly, I think maybe that’s okay. Maybe not every light has to be turned on, maybe not every hand has to reach. Sometimes, you just sit and watch, and hope tomorrow will feel a little easier—like another chance, another look, another light coming through the window.

So, here's the thing: the whole affair started because Mrs. Bell decided she just couldn't stand the smell of horses in the morning anymore. I mean, who could blame her? Imagine the carriages lined up down the lane, all wheels and grumpy drivers and the fog. There was always mist rolling over from the river, like the world was just waking up slow. Anyway, Mrs. Bell marched right over to Mr. Curtis, the head of carriages, or whatever silly thing his title was, and said, "Sir, I would have you know the gentlemen coming to my house aren't to be tripping over your mud."

Now, Mr. Curtis, he was one of those fellows who’d rather talk about the weather than anything real. He tried to smile and doff his hat, said something about "with all due respect ma'am," but Mrs. Bell wasn’t having any of it. She jabbed her umbrella at the nearest wheel, a wobbly old thing, and said, "I expect better." Then she stalked off in a huff, skirts all swooshy.

Funny thing is, the rest of us just watched from the windows. I saw Hamlet, the coach dog—yes, that’s his name—slink behind the boot and sort of squint at the fuss. Hamlet’s got more sense than half the people here, I swear. You ever wonder what dogs think of us when we get all puffed up over mud and manners? Sometimes I think they know something important and just won’t say.

That morning, Osric came by. He's the new gentleman, just in from the city. He's got too-tight boots and the kind of hair that never stays flat, no matter how much he pats it. Osric strolled up with a cocky little grin—like he knew the punchline to a joke no one else heard—and asked Hamlet, "Would you know where a man might find breakfast?" Hamlet sneezed. Osric took it for an answer and headed for the kitchen.

To be honest, the house runs on faith and tea. Mrs. Bell's faith that things will go right, and gallons of tea poured at all hours, mostly by Miss June, the only person who can carry three saucers without dropping one. Miss June says, "If gentlemen'd stop asking for toast at midnight, I’d sleep more." And she laughs, but you can see she means it. Sometimes I help her, carrying the pots up the back stairs, and she tells me who quarreled and who came home cheerful. Feels like being let in on secrets.

And yet, everyone pretends not to know each other's business. Mr. Curtis acts as if Mrs. Bell's umbrella didn't almost puncture his hat. Osric tips imaginary hats to invisible ladies. Hamlet chases crows off the lawn, which he seems to think is some grand quest. The whole house is a stage. I suppose that's true for every house with guests, though—don't you think?

Yesterday, Sir Tamlin came by. He's an old friend of Mrs. Bell, or something more complicated, but no one ever says. His carriage looked like it'd rolled through a hundred puddles. The driver scowled. Sir Tamlin just waltzed in, all smiles, saying, "Faith, my dear, your drive's cost me a shoe." Mrs. Bell sniffed, "At least you’ve one left." They laughed like old soldiers.

So you get to thinking, why do they all come? It's not the food, which is decent but plain, or the view, which mostly involves fog. Maybe it's the peace, the sense that in this little nest, you can be ridiculous and no one will mind. Even Mrs. Bell. Even Osric. There's a moment after supper, when the fire’s low and everyone talks quietly, not because they're hiding things, but because it feels good to rest.

And things just go on, day to day. Carriages in the morning, arguments about mud, gentlemen who can't find their gloves, Hamlet howling at the moon, Miss June cursing the stairs. Maybe nothing much happens. Still, sometimes when I’m tiptoeing down the hall at night, I wonder if deep down, we all know we’re waiting for something. Or is that just what people do in old houses with too many rooms?

So, I gotta just get this out there first—if you’d told me yesterday I was gonna be lost in Ephesus yelling for someone named Dromio, I’d have thought you’d just made up a word. But here I am, and the day honestly started normal. Luciana told me, “You really ought to try the fish stew,” and I guess, yeah, I like to listen, but this time? Wrong move. The market here’s a maze, like, you turn around and it’s just someone new yelling about silk or almonds, and none of the streets are straight. Honestly, how does anyone find anything in this city?

So anyway, I lose Adriana in that crowd. Not on purpose! She was holding my sleeve and then there was that donkey, and poof, she’s gone. I thought, okay, just keep walking, but every time I stopped, some vendor tried to sell me something weirder than the last. Did I look like someone who needed a golden comb? I don’t even have enough hair for a comb. 

The thing is—I heard someone calling for Antipholus, and I thought, well, that’s me, right? But I turn, and it’s this skinny guy with wild eyes, shouting, “Sir! There you are! Luciana’s looking all over!” Now, I swear he looked exactly like our cook’s cousin back home, but I don’t have time to wonder. “Dromio?” I ask, though I’m not even sure. He acts like he’s seen a ghost.

I try to follow him, but then there’s this crowd. Suddenly, everyone’s shouting about a missing purse—wasn’t mine, by the way—and then someone’s pulling at my coat. Am I the only one who can't keep straight who's who? It’s like there’s two of everyone. I see someone who looks like me duck into a side street, and I can’t help but stare. Was it a mirror? No, mirrors don’t wear blue hats.

So yeah, now I’m sitting on some broken steps outside the old bathhouse, just trying to make sense of it all. Luciana comes up, finally, with this look on her face like I’ve forgotten her birthday. “Where have you been?” she says, and I mean, what can I even say to that?

Here’s the thing—do you ever feel like the whole city’s playing a game and you’re the only one who didn’t get the rules? I tried to explain, you know, about the Dromio mix-up, and the lookalike, but Luciana just rolls her eyes. “Everyone says that when they’re late,” she says, like the whole city swaps places for fun. Maybe they do, honestly.

Adriana finally shows up, too, and she’s mad I wandered off. “You said you’d just look at the fruit stall—now the porter says you’ve been in three places at once!” How do I even answer that? Is it possible? I guess today, yeah, it is.

I get up and we start walking back through the square. The sun’s low and everything looks less confusing now that it’s quieter. Luciana’s humming, Adriana keeps glancing over at me—like she’s still not sure I’m the same guy from this morning. Honestly, I’m not totally sure either.

But that’s Ephesus, I suppose. You come for the fish stew, and you end up chasing your own shadow, or someone else’s. And Dromio? Well, he’s probably out there right now, asking some stranger for directions, mixing up names, mixing up faces. Next time, maybe I’ll just stay home. But, really—would that be any less strange?

So, uh, it really started out as one of those days where you can’t tell if the clouds are threatening rain or just teasing you, and believe me, I’ve been fooled before. Anyway, the wharf was unusually loud, gulls screaming at each other about the smallest scraps, and something about the briny stink just made me want to get out on the water, away from all that. Stubb, my—well, I guess you'd call him my right-hand guy, though he'd probably tell you I was his sidekick—he’d already been fussing over the boat for an hour, cursing quietly when the line got tangled up in the anchor chain, you know, like it does every time, and yet he always acts like it’s a surprise. Why do we let ourselves get surprised by the same junk over and over?

So, we finally get the line sorted, and Stubb gives me that look like, “Can we go already, or you wanna stand around watching the clouds argue with the sun all day?” So I hop in, boot hitting the edge just as some tiny fish leaps outta the water right there, like he's got somewhere he needs to be in a hurry, and honestly that just makes me laugh. I don't know what it is about fish, but you can't trust 'em to do what you expect. They're always darting left when you think they'll go right.

Anyway, we push off, and the water's got that look, you know, almost glassy if you squint, but with just enough chop to make you wonder if you're gonna get soaked for your troubles. Stubb starts talking about the whale again—you know, the whale. The big one, the one nobody ever really sees but everyone claims they've seen, like some kind of giant fish-shaped rumor. The thing is, he’s always talking about it, but today he’s got that tone like maybe this’ll be the day. “You see that ripple?” he says, jabbing his oar out at nothing, “That’s not a fish. That’s too round.” He’s convinced, and I try to believe him, but I mean, how many times can you chase a shadow before you start doubting the sun?

We get out far enough that the land's gone soft at the edges, sort of fuzzy, and it’s just us, the boat, and an awful lot of nothing. The line goes out—Stubb insists on it, fussing with the knots, his hands moving faster than his mouth, which is really saying something. I throw in a joke about maybe the whale’ll be hungry today and take the whole boat, and Stubb barks out a laugh but then gets real quiet. It's that kind of silence you can almost lean on.

We wait. There’s the slap of water against the hull, and all the little sounds that sneak up on you out here—wind, ropes, a couple more fish popping up like they want to be noticed and then darting away, and I wonder if they get tired of being chased or if that’s just life when you’re shaped like dinner. Anyway, after a while, Stubb gets antsy and starts winding in the line, muttering that it “don’t feel right.” I pretend not to notice, but I’m watching the way his hands shake just a little, like he’s got a story he’s keeping to himself.

Then, outta nowhere, the boat tips—not enough to be dangerous, but enough to make both our hearts jump. I grip the side and look at Stubb, and he’s staring at the water like it’s got secrets. There’s a bubbly patch right behind us, all round and weirdly calm, and if you asked me then, I’d have said the whole ocean was holding its breath. So—did we see the whale? Or did the whale see us? I still can’t answer, and honestly, I think that’s what keeps us going out there. That and the way the water never looks the same twice.

After nothing else happens, we just sort of drift for a while, listening to the gentle slap of the tide and, uh, convincing ourselves that maybe next time will be the day, you know? By the time we head back, the clouds are finally done playing games and the rain starts real slow, like it doesn’t want to interrupt us, and I just laugh, ‘cause isn’t that always the way? You chase something round and round, thinking you’ll get a straight answer, and end up a little wetter, a little older, maybe just barely closer to whatever you’re after—or maybe not at all. But hey, tomorrow’s another day, and the fish’ll probably be jumping again, and Stubb’ll have a new story, and I guess we’ll just keep following that line, wherever it goes.

So, um, the thing is, Mr. Darcy was standing right in the hallway, kinda just looking out the window like he’d lost his keys or something. Elizabeth, well, she noticed him before he noticed her—she always does, doesn’t she? And honestly, it’s almost like she moves with purpose, even when she’s totally unsure. Who does that? I mean, maybe it’s just something about her, a vibe, I guess.

Anyway, she hesitated for a second, pretending to arrange the flowers on the little table, really just buying herself time. You ever do that? Like, try to look busy when you’re actually just stalling? I swear, it’s human nature. So, Mr. Darcy, he turns, and now they’re both sort of trapped, neither one wanting to speak first. It’s ridiculously awkward, but Elizabeth, she gets this little smile, and then, out of nowhere, says, “Lovely day, isn’t it?” Which is stupid, because it’s raining so hard you can barely see the garden.

He actually laughs, which is kinda rare, if you know him, and then replies, “I suppose it’s lovely in its own way.” I mean, is that flirting? Or just being polite? I can never tell with him. If you’re curious, Mr. Gardiner walks in at that precise moment—he’s always timing things weirdly—and immediately starts talking about dinner being ready and how he hopes the fish isn’t overcooked. Nobody cares about the fish, but it breaks the tension.

Elizabeth, though, she’s thinking a million miles a minute. Not that you’d know by looking at her. She’s wondering if she should ask him about the letter—oh, yeah, that letter. You know, the one Darcy sent her, clearing up everything she thought about him, and Wickham, and all of that drama. But she can’t just blurt it out, right? I mean, who does that? Instead, she stares at the rain and says, “If only the sun would come out, maybe we’d walk.” Is she inviting him? Maybe. Maybe not. Who knows.

Darcy’s just a little off-balance, I think. He says, “I’d walk, regardless of weather.” Which, honestly, is such a Darcy thing to say. You get this feeling he’d walk through a hurricane if Elizabeth was asking. Mrs. Gardiner—who’s much savvier than most people give her credit for—chimes in, “You two can always borrow my umbrella, if you like.” She says it with a wink, and Elizabeth almost blushes, but she covers it by fussing with her sleeve.

So the conversation, if you can call it that, sputters out for a second, and everyone kind of drifts into the dining room. The thing is, nobody actually knows what’s going on between Darcy and Elizabeth. Well, okay, Gardiner suspects, but he won’t say anything. He just serves the fish, which is fine, not amazing, and talks about local gossip. Elizabeth keeps glancing at Darcy, and he catches her eye, then looks away. It’s, um, like they’re both waiting for some silent signal. Has anybody ever figured out how you’re supposed to act in those moments? I sure haven’t.

Dinner goes on, and they’re all talking about travel—Mrs. Gardiner brings up Bath, and Mr. Darcy quietly mentions he’s never really liked crowds. Elizabeth almost laughs, because of course he hasn’t. Then she asks, “Have you seen the gardens here when the roses bloom?” It’s not something she’s genuinely asking, more like she needs to fill the air. Darcy tells her he saw them last year, and, uh, Elizabeth says, “They were probably better then.” Which, you know, isn’t even about flowers. It’s just another way to say things change.

The thing is, they’re both trying to figure out how to say what they mean. Darcy finally, quietly, asks if she’s read his letter. Elizabeth nods, but doesn’t say much else. It’s almost like the words hang in the air, waiting for them to catch up. Mr. Gardiner, meanwhile, is distracting everyone by bringing out some pudding no one really wanted, and Mrs. Gardiner asks Elizabeth if she’ll go for a walk tomorrow. Elizabeth says, “Yes,” and Darcy says he’d like to join too. It’s a little clumsy, but somehow it all fits.

Honestly, if you ask me, I think that’s how real things happen. Not in big declarations, but in little awkward moments, sideways glances, and rain on the window. You know? Would it even be love if it wasn’t weird sometimes? I think not.

So the thing is, there’s always been something off about Catherine, and—wait, I know that sounds unfair, but hear me out. You know how some people just have that look? Like you walk into a room and you can feel someone’s watching, but you just… you can’t tell who because everyone’s being so normal and drinking whatever bland punch somebody brought, but it’s her. And her eyes, I swear, they’re always a little too bright, catching the light in that way that makes you want to look away but you can’t. I don’t know if I’m explaining this right.

It wasn’t like I was obsessed with her, or whatever—you ever get those weird gut feelings, just for no reason? You can’t shake ’em. I’d see her around, standing off near the window or trailing after the so-called "master," old Mr. Jacobs, who ran the place. Nobody called him that out loud, though. We’d just kind of exchange these glances, you know, the kind where you both know there’s a joke that you’re not saying because it’d be too much effort. Anyway, Catherine would watch him, and sometimes I’d catch her lips moving just a bit, but I couldn’t hear anything, not really.

One afternoon, after most people went out to get lunch, I hung back, pretending to be lost in some crap about supply orders just to avoid the heat outside. Catherine stayed behind too, sitting at one of the desks flipping an old book—looked like the pages were about to fall out. I was about to ask her what she was reading, not really wanting an answer or caring, but instead I just kind of blurted, “Do you ever get tired of this place?” and, wow, why’d I say that? She looked up, real slow, and for a second I thought maybe she’d just ignore me like usual, but she sort of smiled in this way that didn’t really reach her eyes and said, “Sometimes I imagine I’m somewhere else. Somewhere with fewer clocks.”

Isn’t that a weird answer? I mean, what was I supposed to say? There weren’t even that many clocks in the office—three, tops, unless you counted the old grandfather clock that hadn’t worked in years. Sometimes I saw her standing in front of it, though, like she was waiting for it to start ticking again, which is… I don’t know, odd?

Now, here’s the part that sticks with me. A few days later, everyone was buzzing because Mr. Jacobs had lost his glasses and was wandering around half-blind as if the building itself had turned against him. Catherine didn’t say a word, but she had this look that made me think she knew exactly where they were. And later, when I saw her alone in the stairwell, holding those very glasses, she just pressed a finger to her lips like she was telling me to keep quiet, as if it mattered to anyone but him.

I don’t know why, but suddenly I got the urge to ask her if she was happy. I know, it’s none of my business, right? But I did it anyway, kind of mumbling it, half-hoping she wouldn’t hear. But she did. She nodded, slow, and said, “Sometimes, when nobody’s looking, I imagine I’m the one giving orders.”

What does that even mean? I thought about it all day, but I couldn’t get it out of my head. Was she talking about Mr. Jacobs? Or someone else—maybe herself? And honestly, I know I should’ve just left it, but once you start noticing stuff, you can’t un-notice it. Like, I’d catch Catherine in the reflection of the front doors, watching everyone go by, her face all unreadable, and I started wondering if everyone else saw it too, or if it was just me seeing another version of her, one that was waiting for something.

I’m not saying she was dangerous or anything dramatic like that. If anything, she seemed tired, like she was waiting for life to let her in on the big secret. I get that. Who isn’t, sometimes? Still, there’s something that happens when you realize someone’s always in the background, holding on to stuff nobody else knows about—including, apparently, people’s glasses—and yet, they never seem to want the spotlight. Or do they? That’s the thing, right? How can you tell what people really want when you can barely sort out what you want yourself?

So I guess now, every time I run into Catherine, I wonder if she’s still watching, still keeping tabs on everyone, or if she’s finally found a place with fewer clocks and more time for herself. Or maybe, just maybe, she’s the real master after all, and we just haven’t caught on yet

So, uh, let me try and tell you about Timon—yeah, Timon of, well, let's just say from Athens, but it hardly matters where he's from, right? It's not like that stuff sticks with you after you've heard his story. The thing is, Timon started off the kind of friend everyone thinks they want. If you’d met him first, you’d probably think, wow, this guy would give you anything, maybe even his last loaf. And that was true. Almost too true, if I’m being honest.

The thing with Timon is, he didn’t see it coming. Like, not even a hint. His house—it was always open, like, wide open, and if—if you happened to come by hungry or broke or just plain bored, he’d find a way to help. He’d be pulling out coins, food, even little gifts for your kids or whatever. And he laughed easy, like someone who didn’t know there was such a thing as a bad friend.

But you know what happens, right? Or wait, maybe you don’t, but you can probably guess. People talk about Athens being a city where folks look out for each other, but, honestly, if you looked close, it was mostly looking out for themselves. And for a while, Timon didn’t notice. Or maybe he didn’t care. Maybe he thought, like, someday I’ll need a hand and they’ll be there.

Well, the day came. It always does, doesn’t it? I mean, isn’t that the way—first you give, then one day you gotta ask, and that’s when you see what’s what. Anyway, Timon’s luck turned. I couldn’t say how, exactly—maybe he spent too much, maybe thieves, maybe the cost of throwing feast after feast actually bites—doesn’t matter much. Bottom line, he finds himself without, uh, anything. Not even enough for bread. So he knocks on those same doors he kept open so wide, and guess what he gets? Nothing. Not a crumb, not a coin, not even a polite lie.

He tried to laugh it off the first time. “Ah, you must be busy,” he’d say, or, “Next time, then,” and wave and try another friend. The thing is, after a while, you run out of friends to try. Turns out, the word “friend” is easy to use when you’re full and comfortable and the wine hasn’t run out, but it gets real heavy when there’s nothing left to take. Am I making sense? I’m just saying, he realized he was alone in that city, and not just alone, but—what’s worse—forgotten.

So, Timon gets angry. No, not just angry. He turns into someone else entirely. He stops trusting, stops talking, and, uh, I guess you could say he stops living, really. He leaves Athens. Just walks out. Some people said they saw him, dirty and wild, digging up roots to eat. Maybe he’d found gold in the ground once—some folks say that much—but who cares? It’s not about the gold. The whole point is, no one followed him.

And, I mean, can you blame him? If you gave everything away and then when you needed so much as a crust, nobody came, wouldn’t you feel, I don’t know, small and used-up? Do you ever wonder if anyone really means it when they say, “I’ll be there for you”? Timon did. He wondered, and then he stopped wondering, and then he just stopped.

Now, I’m not saying Athens changed without him. Probably didn’t. A city like that, it rolls on. But maybe, somewhere, someone remembered the way he used to laugh, or the way he used to call everyone “friend”—even folks he barely knew. Maybe. Or maybe not. Doesn’t change much, I guess. Just—if you happen to have a friend who gives first, maybe check in once in a while. You know, before the asking gets hard and there’s nothing left but, well, regret.

So, like, the thing is, people always talk about gods like they're these distant beings, right? Floating up there, watching us, maybe bored, maybe angry, whatever, but I don't know, I kind of think it's way messier than that. I mean, if gods actually cared about men, or about the stupid little stuff we do, you'd think they'd make themselves a bit clearer. But all we ever get is hints, or weird signs, or someone’s grandma seeing a vision in her oatmeal. Sometimes, though, you've gotta wonder—are they really just messing with us for fun? Because, sitting in the public square on game day, watching the whole city lose its mind over some team of strangers, it feels like we're all puppets, dancing for someone else's amusement. Maybe that's what the games are for—just another way to keep us distracted, to make sure nobody notices what's actually happening behind the scenes.

I remember once, when I was a kid, I snuck behind the stadium with my cousin, thinking we'd find the players' secret hangout or something cool. Instead, we saw this weird ritual—like, there was this old guy, might've been a guard or a janitor, and he was lighting candles and mumbling, and honestly, I couldn't understand half of it, but he looked scared, not just respectful-scared, but actually freaked out. He was doing it for someone, or something, I guess, maybe hoping the gods would leave him alone. We didn't tell anyone, obviously, 'cause what if it's normal? What if everyone who works there has to do something wicked just to keep the games going? My cousin said it's a secret tradition passed down, and that's how the city stays lucky, which sounds like nonsense, but who really knows?

That was years ago, but things haven't gotten any clearer. Sometimes I sit at those games, surrounded by screaming people, and I wonder—do the gods sit among us, disguised as regular folks, eating popcorn and laughing at our bad plays? Or maybe they're just watching on their own, bored and kinda annoyed that we still care so much about who wins or loses. You'd think, after centuries, someone would've figured it all out, cracked the code, made the gods reveal themselves, but nope. Men just keep hoping, and praying, and inventing new ways to please whatever might be out there.

One night, not too long ago, I was walking through the city after midnight, and everything was quiet except the occasional stray cat and the distant sound of music from some bar. I saw this guy, dressed in fancy clothes but looking totally lost, just staring up at the statues in the plaza. I didn't mean to stare, but he looked different, like the kind of person who knows something nobody else does. He caught my eye and gave this crooked smile, then whispered, "You ever wonder if it's all just a game for them?" I didn't answer—what could I say?—but the question stuck with me. If that's the case, then what's the point? Are we just pieces on a board, moved around whenever the gods get bored?

Anyway, the thing is, secrets are everywhere, but most folks pretend not to see them. You see strange stuff, like a man leaving offerings behind a trash bin, or a kid drawing weird symbols in chalk before skipping rope, and you wonder if it's just superstition or if there's something deeper. Maybe everyone knows a little bit, but we're all too scared to admit it. Like, who wants to be the person who says, "Hey, I saw something that might mean the gods are real, and they've got their own rules"? Nobody does. Because the public likes things simple—cheering, betting, arguing about scores. Anything odd is just ignored, pushed away. I guess that's safer, even if it feels fake sometimes.

So, I don't really have answers, and that's probably obvious by now, but I keep thinking about that old man by the stadium, the fancy guy in the plaza, and all the weird little rituals that seem harmless—or wicked, depending on your mood. Maybe the gods see everything, maybe they don't care, maybe they're just waiting for us to do something interesting. Is that why the games matter so much, even though they shouldn't? I don't know. I just know that if you really look, if you pay attention, you’ll see things nobody else wants to see, and honestly, I'm not sure that's a good thing.

So, uh, the thing is, Alice didn't exactly expect her afternoon would end up like this. I mean, who really plans to be sitting on a jagged rock beside a weeping turtle and a feather-bristled gryphon that couldn't stop interrupting? Not her, that's for sure. And, to make it stranger, the sun's kind of hanging low, dripping through the clouds, painting everything that odd orange-pink that makes you feel a bit off balance, but in a way that's almost pleasant if you just let it be. 

"Soup's not all that bad, you know," the Gryphon said, tilting its head and scratching under its beak with a claw that looked pretty dangerous. You wouldn't want to be a mouse around that thing, Alice thought, but didn't say anything because, honestly, it seemed rude.

"But it could've been beautiful," the Mock Turtle sniffed, blinking tears from eyes so watery it seemed like they might just pour onto the beach and make everything even more soggy. "I always thought, if only I'd had parsley, or maybe a dash of patience, things would have been different."

Alice shuffled, her shoes all gritty from the pebbles. "Patience? Can you really add that to soup?”

The Gryphon barked—kind of a laugh, kind of a cough. "Shows what you know. Patience goes with everything, 'specially soup."

"And yet," said the Mock Turtle, and it sounded almost wise, the way old people do when they're telling you about how biscuits used to be thicker, "patience doesn't make it less salty, or give it any friends. I would've liked some friends."

Alice, not really sure what to say, poked a stick at the foam around her toes. "You have us," she tried.

"But are you friends or just, uh, flavor?" the Mock Turtle said, blinking.

She didn't know how to answer that. Who would? Are you a friend, or are you just passing through, picking up a bit of oddness before you go home and tell your cat about it? And the answer doesn't really seem to matter to the Gryphon, who's flapping its wings and sending a few stray feathers into the air, like it's shedding its worries one by one. If only people could do that.

"Well, what if," Alice started and stopped, because she wasn't entirely sure what she wanted to ask. "What if you could make any soup you liked, and it could be as beautiful as you want—would you still want someone to share it with?"

The Mock Turtle thought about this for a long moment, his shell reflecting the weird colors of the sunset. A seagull, fat and bold, landed nearby and eyed them all, probably hoping for crumbs.

"I think," said the Mock Turtle, "I'd want someone to taste it, so they'd tell me whether it was too sweet or too hot, or if maybe I'd done too much celery again."

"Yeah, and then you could argue about it," the Gryphon chipped in, sounding delighted by the idea. "Nothin' better than a good argument over soup. It's tradition where I'm from."

Alice kind of laughed, because she could picture her sister arguing with her about what should go in the sandwich, or if the jam was too lumpy. There's always someone who wants things just so.

"But," Alice said, more quietly, "what if they didn't like it? Or what if nobody wanted to try it at all?"

The Gryphon, for once, didn't have an answer. Instead, it just looked at Alice, its eyes a sort of muddy gold, like it was trying to see what she was really asking.

"It's a risk," the Mock Turtle said, and you could tell he'd been thinking about this his whole life—even if turtle lives weren't what she was used to. "But I'd rather try. It's lonelier to know nobody tasted at all, even if they didn't like it."

For a long time, none of them spoke, just listened to the soft flap of the Gryphon's wings and the distant slap of waves on the shore. The sun kept dipping, and the air felt cooler, and Alice wondered if she'd ever think about soup the same way again. Maybe she'd go home and make some—she wasn't sure what kind, or how it would turn out—but she thought, if she did, she might ask someone to taste it with her, and not worry too much if they made a face or suggested more salt. 

Isn't it strange, how you can sit between a crying turtle and a feathered lion-bird, and end up feeling like maybe, just maybe, you know a little more about what friendship means?

Right, so picture this: there’s this one night—the kind where you can hardly tell if the sky is mad at you or just bored—when the old bark’s groaning from the bottom of her keel up, and everyone’s pretending not to notice. The sea’s got that slapping sound, you know, like someone trying to wake up a corpse, and the whole ship’s shivering even though it’s not that cold, not really. Anyway, I was standing there—well, leaning, if we’re being honest, ‘cause my legs were numb and my feet were soaked—right by the rail, and that’s when Ahab came stomping out, wild-eyed as a storm.

Now, the thing is, when Ahab sets his jaw, no one asks questions. It’s like, you see that face, and you just—well, you mind your own business, plain and simple. But Stubb, of all people, he just had to pipe up, didn’t he? Said something about the moon being cut in two, like maybe even it was afraid of what’s coming. I couldn’t tell if he was joking or if he really thought there was something up there that’d split the moon. Sometimes it’s hard to say with Stubb.

So, we’re standing there, everyone silent except for the wind and the sound of the ropes twitching like they’re itching to get loose, and Ahab started pacing. If you’ve not seen it, let me just say—the man doesn’t really walk. It’s more of a march, but with one leg that never quite catches up, so everything he touches, the deck, the rigging, the planks beneath your feet, it all vibrates with this—I dunno—this anger that’s almost alive. Who’s angry at whom, though? The ship or the man or the sea? Don’t ask me.

Then suddenly, he stopped. Just stopped, right in front of the forward hatch. And he stared out at the swell—big, black, like a city built of water moving under us—and he says, “Blows, there. D’ye see it?” And, sure enough, off the port bow, there’s this plume in the moonlight, like a ghost breathing. We all crowded over, nearly tipping the whole damn ship trying to see. I’m betting even the rats came out for a look.

And honestly, you could feel something change then, in the air, as if the ocean had been holding its breath and just then decided to let it out. Someone—I think it was Flask, but don’t quote me—muttered, “We’ve found him.” Like that’s what we’d been looking for all along, as if we hadn’t spent weeks going in circles, chasing shadows on water.

You ever get that feeling when you know you’re about to do something stupid but you can’t stop yourself? That’s how it was. Not one of us thought to ask, “Should we?” We just tightened belts, checked knives, and tried to look braver than we were.

There’s this weird thing that happens on ships, or maybe just on this ship. When the sky’s black enough and the sea’s loud enough, words start to sound like lies, so you keep quiet. You listen for orders, sure, but really you’re listening to see if the sea’s gonna offer up some secret, or if tonight’s the night she decides to swallow the whole lot of us. Is that superstition? I dunno. Maybe it’s just that people have to believe in something when everything else is wet and shifting and unreliable.

Stubb kept cracking jokes. He couldn’t help himself. “Maybe the whale’s come to take us to a dance,” he said, winking, and you couldn’t decide whether to laugh or push him overboard. Ahab just looked at him like he was made of salt and vanished in the dark.

Thing is, when someone—doesn’t matter who—yells, “There she blows!” every single heart on board slams shut. It’s a kind of fear, I guess, but mixed with hope too, but also a bit of—I’m gonna say it—greed. Like everyone’s thinking, “Maybe it’ll be different for me.” Never is, but there you have it.

The rest of the night? Well, it went the way it always does—rope burns, barking commands, shadows that look like monsters until the sun comes up and shows you it’s only your own hand. By dawn, we were all older and none the wiser, and the sea—she just kept rolling, like she’d never seen us at all.

You know, I’ve always thought people talk too much about things they know nothing about—like, really, if you look at last night at Netherfield, who saw anything? No one. Everyone just guesses, and, well, they act like it’s knowledge. But, the thing is, I was there, just sitting by the fireplace pretending to ignore everyone else, when Lizzy came in—you know, with her muddied skirt and all that—and, I swear, there was a hush, just for a second. Not dramatic, just—like everyone noticed something but didn’t want to admit it out loud.

Mrs. Bennet, of course, can’t keep quiet when she feels she has an audience. “My dear Jane,” she cried—really too loud for a drawing room—“if Mr. Bingley doesn’t see how devoted you are, then, truly, nothing in the world makes sense.” And Jane just kind of smiled, polite as ever, but I saw her look down at her hands. Maybe she was nervous, or maybe she just wanted everyone to stop talking for once.

Oh, and Bingley was… well, he’s always nice. I mean, almost confusingly nice, if that makes any sense. Is it possible for someone to be too agreeable? Sometimes I wonder if he has any opinions at all. Like, he just laughed at whatever anyone said, fiddled with his cuffs, and asked after the weather—again. Poor Jane tried to answer every question like it was the first time, though Lizzy shot her a look that said, “Don’t encourage him.” Not that Bingley minded. I think he’d be happy if every conversation was sort of about nothing, just floating along.

And then you’ve got Darcy—well, he stood in the corner. Really, he only talked a bit, mostly to Lizzy, and even then, it was like every word cost him a penny. You could kind of see Lizzy’s eyebrow going up as she listened, but she never lost her cool. She never does. Actually, I’m convinced she’d argue with a thunderstorm, if she thought it was being unreasonable.

Honestly, sometimes I think the people in that room must be living in a different world than I am. I mean, do they really believe what they’re saying? All that stuff about happiness and good fortune and—what was it Bingley said? “Cheerful company is the greatest delight.” As if that explains anything, or means anything at all. Maybe I’m just being grumpy. Maybe I should’ve had more lemonade.

But it gets better—or worse, depending on how you look at it. Mrs. Bennet started talking about the entail (again), and I thought, “If she says something about cousins, I’ll run into the rain.” And Jane just sat there, patient, like she was bracing herself for a storm, but Mary piped up about ‘moral worth’ (whatever that is), and the whole thing drifted away. Are people really listening to each other, or just waiting for their turn?

Oh, and did I mention how Kitty sneezed—like, three times in a row? No one said “bless you.” Everyone just stared, and then it went on as if nothing happened. I guess that’s how it always is. Stuff happens, and we all pretend it didn’t.

But, you know, after the tea and the little speeches and poor Jane trying not to look tired, Lizzy caught my eye and grinned, just for a split second. Like, a real grin—not one of those “I’m fine, everything’s fine” smiles, but more like, “Isn’t this whole thing ridiculous?” And suddenly, I didn’t mind being there so much. Sometimes having someone who gets the joke makes everything else bearable.

So yeah, maybe nothing really happened last night, and everybody’s just talking because it’s easier than saying, “I don’t know.” Or maybe that’s how things move forward—one awkward conversation at a time. Who knows? I’m just glad Lizzy was there.

So, there was this kind of—well, I guess you could call it a gathering, though really, it was more like a collection of people thrown together for reasons that didn’t make much sense, at least not to me. Zossimov, who always looked like he needed another coffee, stood by the window, fiddling with the latch as if it was the most interesting thing in the room. He wasn’t really listening, or maybe he was, but you never could tell with him. That guy’s face always seemed to say, “I’m here, but also, I’m somewhere else.” Anyway, the whole place felt kind of tense, like everyone was waiting for something, though nobody was sure what.
